title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:dimensions}
For $N \ge 3$, $\dim \Phi_N = \dim \Psi_N = N-2$, $\mathcal{L}: \Phi_N \to \Psi_N$ is a bijection, and Assumption~\ref{ass:unisolvence} holds if and only if the matrix $\mathbf{A}$ of \eqref{eq:square_system} is nonsingular.
head: environment
name: Dimensions

title: Proof
body_md: With $s_j = \sin(j\theta_0)$ as in Section~\ref{sec:constants}, one has $w_j(0) = \sqrt{2/\tilde L}\,s_j$ and $w_j(L) = \sqrt{2/\tilde L}\sin(j\pi - j\pi\delta/\tilde L) = (-1)^{j+1}\sqrt{2/\tilde L}\,s_j$. The matrix of the two boundary functionals $v \mapsto v(0)$, $v \mapsto v(L)$ restricted to $\operatorname{span}\{w_1,w_2\}$ is therefore $\sqrt{2/\tilde L}\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} s_1 & s_2 \\ s_1 & -s_2\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, with determinant $-4s_1s_2/\tilde L \ne 0$ because $0 < \pi\delta/\tilde L < 2\pi\delta/\tilde L < \pi$. Hence the two functionals are linearly independent on $V_N$ and $\dim\Phi_N = N-2$. If $v \in \Phi_N$ and $\mathcal{L} v = 0$ then $v = 0$ on $\bar I$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:dirichlet_1d}(i), hence $v = 0$ in $V_N$, since its polynomial factor in Lemma~\ref{lem:chebyshev_variable} vanishes on $[-c_0,c_0]$; so $\mathcal{L}$ is injective on $\Phi_N$, and $\dim\Psi_N = \dim\Phi_N$. Finally, $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = 0$ means that $v := \sum_jc_jw_j$ lies in $\Phi_N$ and that $\mathcal{L} v \in \Psi_N$ vanishes at the interior nodes. Under Assumption~\ref{ass:unisolvence} this forces $\mathcal{L} v = 0$, hence $v = 0$ and $\mathbf{c} = 0$. Conversely, if $\mathbf{A}$ is nonsingular and $\mathcal{L} v$, $v \in \Phi_N$, vanishes at the interior nodes, then the coefficient vector of $v$ lies in the kernel of $\mathbf{A}$, so $v = 0$; interpolation at the $N-2$ interior nodes is therefore injective on the $(N-2)$-dimensional space $\Psi_N$, hence unisolvent.

name: Unisolvence Criterion for the Poisson Operator

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $K_N := \{\psi \in V_N : \psi(x_m) = 0,\ 2 \le m \le N-1\}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:chebyshev_variable}, $\psi \in V_N$ has the form $\sqrt{2/\tilde L}\sin\theta\,q(z)$ with $q \in \mathbb P_{N-1}$, and $\psi \in K_N$ if and only if $q$ vanishes at the $N-2$ distinct points $z_2, \dots, z_{N-1}$ (as $\sin\theta_m \ne 0$), i.e.\ $q = w_N^\circ\cdot(\alpha z + \beta)$; hence $K_N = \operatorname{span}\{\psi_0, \psi_1\}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:dimensions}, $\dim\Psi_N = N-2$, so Assumption~\ref{ass:unisolvence} is equivalent to $\Psi_N \cap K_N = \{0\}$.

Let $(Rv)(x) := v(L-x)$. In the variable $\theta$ this is $\theta \mapsto \pi-\theta$, so $z \mapsto -z$, and $Rw_j = (-1)^{j+1}w_j$: $R$ maps $V_N$ and $\Phi_N$ onto themselves, commutes with $\mathcal{L}_P$ and $\tilde\mathcal{L}_P^{-1}$ on $V_N$, and hence maps $\Psi_N = \mathcal{L}_P(\Phi_N)$ onto itself; since $x_{N+1-m} = L - x_m$, it also maps $K_N$ onto itself. As $w_N^\circ(-z) = (-1)^N w_N^\circ(z)$, one has $R\psi_0 = (-1)^N\psi_0$ and $R\psi_1 = (-1)^{N+1}\psi_1$. If $\Psi_N \cap K_N$ contains $\psi = \alpha\psi_0 + \beta\psi_1 \ne 0$, then, being $R$-invariant, it contains $\tfrac12(\psi \pm R\psi)$, i.e.\ $\alpha\psi_0$ and $\beta\psi_1$, so it contains $\psi_0$ or $\psi_1$; the converse is trivial. Thus Assumption~\ref{ass:unisolvence} fails if and only if $\psi_0 \in \Psi_N$ or $\psi_1 \in \Psi_N$.

For $\psi \in V_N$ put $v := \tilde\mathcal{L}_P^{-1}\psi \in V_N$; then $\psi \in \Psi_N$ if and only if $v \in \Phi_N$, i.e.\ $v(0) = v(L) = 0$, because $\mathcal{L}_P: V_N \to V_N$ is a bijection. If $R\psi = \pm\psi$ then $Rv = \pm v$ and $v(L) = \pm v(0)$, so $\psi \in \Psi_N$ if and only if $v(0) = 0$. Finally $v(0) = \int_{\tilde I}\tilde G(0,y)\psi(y)\,dy$, because $\tilde G$ inverts $-d^2/dx^2$ with Dirichlet conditions on $\tilde I$ and the $w_j$ are its eigenfunctions with eigenvalues $\lambda_j$. Applying this to $\psi_0$ and $\psi_1$ gives \eqref{eq:unisolvence_criterion}.

label: rem:peclet
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:peclet}
The ratio $k/\mu_j$ in \eqref{eq:phase} is a modal P\'eclet number. Convection shifts the phases of all modes of the test space $\Psi_N(k) := \mathcal{L}_{CD}(\Phi_N)$ relative to those of $\Psi_N(0) = \mathcal{L}_P(\Phi_N)$, by $\vartheta_j \le k\tilde L/(j\pi)$, substantially only those of the convection-dominated modes $j \lesssim k\tilde L/\pi$. The ill-conditioning of the frame is a property of its high modes: heuristically, the modes above the transition index $NL/\tilde L$ are those whose restrictions to $I$ are nearly linearly dependent (Section~\ref{sec:potential}). For $N \gg k\tilde L/\pi$ these modes are the same in $\Psi_N(k)$ and $\Psi_N(0)$ up to phase shifts $O(k\tilde L/N)$, so the interpolation operators of the two test spaces can be expected to have the same ill-conditioning and, by \eqref{eq:GN_entries}, the discrete Green's functions the same structure; the exact computations of Section~\ref{sec:num_1d} find nearly the same exponential rate of $\Lambda_N^\Psi$ for $k \le 50$. For $N \lesssim k\tilde L/\pi$ convection reshapes the whole test space; in the experiments of Section~\ref{sec:num_solvers} with $k$ up to $10^5$ the convergence rate is nevertheless unchanged, and only the floor of the unnormalized system rises, with the norm of the matrix. The physical upstream decay of $G_{CD}$ is a low-mode property, and the interpolation error $f - \mathcal{P}_N f$, the only quantity on which $\mathcal{L}^{-1}$ acts by Corollary~\ref{cor:error}, is concentrated in the high modes, on which $\mathcal{L}_{CD}^{-1}$ and $\mathcal{L}_P^{-1}$ act alike: the moduli of their symbols $1/(\mu_j^2 + ik\mu_j)$ and $1/\mu_j^2$ agree to relative accuracy $(k/\mu_j)^2/2$, and their phases differ by $\vartheta_j$.

Heuristically, for variable $k$ the high modes of $\Psi_N$ are perturbations of those of $\Psi_N(0)$ of relative size $O(\lVertk\rVert_\infty\tilde L/(j\pi))$, so that the conclusion of Remark~\ref{rem:peclet} can be expected to persist; the variable-coefficient experiment of Section~\ref{sec:num_2d} agrees with this.

title: Proof
body_md: Put $\mathcal{P}_N := 0$ for $2 \le N < N_1$. For $N \ge N_1$, $\mathcal{P}_N f$ depends only on the values of $f$ at the interior nodes, hence only on its values on the equispaced $N$-point grid $x_1, \dots, x_N$ of $\bar I$; therefore $\{\mathcal{P}_N\}_{N\ge2}$ is an approximation procedure based on equispaced grids in the sense of \cite[Sec.~1]{platte2011impossibility}, transferred from $[-1,1]$ to $\bar I$ by the affine map. For $N \ge N_1$, since $\mathcal{P}_N$ is linear and its Lagrange functions are real, its condition number \cite[Eq.~(1.1)]{platte2011impossibility}, the supremum over complex nodal data of the ratio between the maximum norm of the output on $\bar I$ and the maximum norm of the data, is $\max_{x\in\bar I}\sum_m|\ell_m^\Psi(x)| = \Lambda_N^\Psi$. Let $E'$ be a compact set with $E \subset \operatorname{int}E'$. Every function continuous on $E'$ and analytic in its interior is analytic in a neighbourhood of $E$ and satisfies $\lVertf\rVert_{L^\infty(E)} \le \lVertf\rVert_{L^\infty(E')}$, so the hypothesis, together with $\lVertf\rVert_{L^\infty(I)} \le \lVertf\rVert_{L^\infty(E')}$ for $N < N_1$, gives $\lVertf - \mathcal{P}_N f\rVert_{L^\infty(I)} \le C'\sigma^{-N}\lVertf\rVert_{L^\infty(E')}$ for all such $f$ and all $N \ge 2$, with $C' := \max\{C, \sigma^{N_1}\}$; this is hypothesis (3.1) of \cite[Thm.~3.1]{platte2011impossibility} for the set $E'$. That theorem yields $\beta > 1$ and $N_0 \ge N_1$ with $\Lambda_N^\Psi \ge \beta^N$ for all $N \ge N_0$. Since $\Lambda_N^\Psi \ge 1$ for every $N \ge N_1$ (each Lagrange function equals one at its node), the claim holds for all $N \ge N_1$ with $c := \min\{1, \min_{N_1 \le N < N_0}\Lambda_N^\Psi\beta^{-N}\}$.

By \eqref{eq:GN_entries}, row $i$ of $\mathbf{G}_N$ consists of the moments of the Lagrange functions $\ell_m^\Psi$ against the fixed kernel $G(x_i,\cdot)$. For a well-conditioned interpolation space $\lVert\ell_m^\Psi\rVert_{L^1} \approx h$, and $\mathbf{G}_N$ inherits the continuous kernel, $(\mathbf{G}_N)_{im} \approx h\,G(x_i,x_m)$; here the masses are exponentially large, and the rows of $\mathbf{G}_N$ follow their profile for both operators (Section~\ref{sec:num_greens}). title: Lemma

name: The Node Potential in Closed Form

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1: reduction to $(0,\theta_0)$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:cl2}(iv) and the substitution $\varphi \mapsto \pi - \varphi$, which maps $(\pi - \theta_0, \pi)$ onto $(0, \theta_0)$ and $\cos\varphi$ to $-\cos\varphi$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\theta_0}^{\pi-\theta_0}\log|\cos\theta - \cos\varphi|\,d\varphi &= -\pi\log 2 \\
&\quad - \int_0^{\theta_0}\bigl(\log|\cos\theta - \cos\varphi| + \log|\cos\theta + \cos\varphi|\bigr)\,d\varphi .
\end{aligned}
\]

\emph{Step 2: evaluation.} By
\[
\cos\theta - \cos\varphi = -2\sin\tfrac{\theta+\varphi}{2}\,\sin\tfrac{\theta-\varphi}{2}, \qquad
\cos\theta + \cos\varphi = 2\sin\tfrac{\pi-\theta-\varphi}{2}\,\sin\tfrac{\pi-\theta+\varphi}{2},
\]
each of the two logarithms equals $-\log 2$ plus two terms of the form $\log|2\sin(t/2)|$. With $\mathrm{Cl}_2(b) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(a) = -\int_a^b\log|2\sin(t/2)|\,dt$, the evenness of the integrand, and the substitutions $t = \theta \pm \varphi$ and $t = \pi - \theta \pm \varphi$,
\begin{align*}
\int_0^{\theta_0}\log\bigl|2\sin\tfrac{\theta+\varphi}{2}\bigr|\,d\varphi &= \mathrm{Cl}_2(\theta) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(\theta+\theta_0), \\
\int_0^{\theta_0}\log\bigl|2\sin\tfrac{\theta-\varphi}{2}\bigr|\,d\varphi &= \mathrm{Cl}_2(\theta-\theta_0) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(\theta), \\
\int_0^{\theta_0}\log\bigl|2\sin\tfrac{\pi-\theta-\varphi}{2}\bigr|\,d\varphi &= \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-\theta-\theta_0) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-\theta), \\
\int_0^{\theta_0}\log\bigl|2\sin\tfrac{\pi-\theta+\varphi}{2}\bigr|\,d\varphi &= \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-\theta) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-\theta+\theta_0).
\end{align*}
The four right-hand sides add up to the bracket $[\cdots]$ of \eqref{eq:U_closed}, so the integral in Step~1 equals $-\pi\log 2 + 2\theta_0\log 2 - [\cdots] = -\omega\log 2 - [\cdots]$, and $U_\omega(\cos\theta) = -\omega^{-1}$ times this integral is \eqref{eq:U_closed}.

\emph{Step 3: special values.} At $\theta = 0$ the bracket is $-2\mathrm{Cl}_2(\theta_0) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-\theta_0) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi+\theta_0) = 2\bigl[\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-\theta_0) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(\theta_0)\bigr] = -\mathrm{Cl}_2(2\theta_0)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cl2}(i) and (ii), and $2\theta_0 = \pi-\omega$. At $\theta = \theta_0$ it is $-\mathrm{Cl}_2(2\theta_0) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-2\theta_0) = \mathrm{Cl}_2(\omega) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-\omega) = \tfrac12\mathrm{Cl}_2(2\omega)$ by (i), $\mathrm{Cl}_2(0) = 0$ and (ii). At $\theta = \pi/2$ it is $2\bigl[\mathrm{Cl}_2(\omega/2) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-\omega/2)\bigr] = \mathrm{Cl}_2(\omega)$ by (ii). This proves \eqref{eq:U_values}.

\emph{Step 4: monotonicity.} Differentiating \eqref{eq:U_closed} with $\mathrm{Cl}_2'(x) = -\log|2\sin(x/2)|$ and combining the four logarithms with $2\sin a\cos a = \sin 2a$ gives, for $0 < \theta < \pi/2$, $\theta \ne \theta_0$,
\[
\frac{d}{d\theta}U_\omega(\cos\theta) = \frac{1}{\omega}\log\frac{\sin(\theta+\theta_0)}{|\sin(\theta-\theta_0)|} .
\]
For such $\theta$, both $|\theta - \theta_0|$ and $\min\{\theta+\theta_0, \pi-\theta-\theta_0\}$ lie in $[0,\pi/2]$, and the second exceeds the first because $\theta, \theta_0 > 0$ and $2\max\{\theta,\theta_0\} < \pi$; as $\sin$ is increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ and $\sin(\theta+\theta_0) = \sin(\pi-\theta-\theta_0)$, the derivative is positive. The function $\theta \mapsto U_\omega(\cos\theta)$ is continuous (the derivative has an integrable singularity at $\theta_0$) and hence increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$, and \eqref{eq:U_closed} is invariant under $\theta \mapsto \pi-\theta$; this proves the remaining claims.

Since $s(\omega) + s(\pi-\omega) = 1$ and $a(\omega) + a(\pi-\omega) = 1$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:duality}), the function $a - s$ is odd about $\pi/2$ and vanishes there, so it suffices to prove $a(\omega) > s(\omega)$ for $\omega \in (\pi/2,\pi)$. Put $x := \pi - \omega \in (0,\pi/2)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cl2}(i), $\mathrm{Cl}_2(2\omega) = \mathrm{Cl}_2(2\pi - 2x) = -\mathrm{Cl}_2(2x)$, so \eqref{eq:exponent} reads
\[
a(\omega) = \frac{\mathrm{Cl}_2(x) - \tfrac12\mathrm{Cl}_2(2x)}{\mathrm{Cl}_2(x) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi - x)}, \qquad s(\omega) = \frac{x}{\pi} .
\]
The Clausen function is positive on $(0,\pi)$: its derivative $-\log(2\sin(t/2))$ is positive on $(0,\pi/3)$ and negative on $(\pi/3,\pi)$, and $\mathrm{Cl}_2(0) = \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi) = 0$. Hence the denominator is positive, and $a(\omega) > s(\omega)$ is equivalent to $\pi\bigl[\mathrm{Cl}_2(x) - \tfrac12\mathrm{Cl}_2(2x)\bigr] > x\bigl[\mathrm{Cl}_2(x) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-x)\bigr]$. By the duplication formula of Lemma~\ref{lem:cl2}(ii), $\tfrac12\mathrm{Cl}_2(2x) = \mathrm{Cl}_2(x) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi - x)$, so the left-hand side equals $\pi\,\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi - x)$, and the inequality becomes
\[
D(x) := (\pi - x)\,\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi - x) - x\,\mathrm{Cl}_2(x) > 0, \qquad 0 < x < \pi/2 .
\]
The function $D$ is continuous on $[0,\pi/2]$ with $D(0) = \pi\,\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi) = 0$ and $D(\pi/2) = 0$. On $(0,\pi/2)$ it is twice differentiable, and with $\mathrm{Cl}_2'(y) = -\log(2\sin(y/2))$ one finds $D'(x) = -\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-x) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(x) + (\pi - x)\log(2\cos(x/2)) + x\log(2\sin(x/2))$ and
\begin{gather*}
D''(x) = 2\log\tan\frac x2 + \frac12\Bigl[x\cot\frac x2 - (\pi - x)\tan\frac x2\Bigr] = F(x/2), \\
F(u) := 2\log\tan u + u\cot u - \Bigl(\frac\pi2 - u\Bigr)\tan u .
\end{gather*}
Here $F(\pi/4) = 0$ and, for $0 < u < \pi/4$,
\begin{gather*}
F'(u) = \frac{3}{\sin u\cos u} - \frac{u}{\sin^2u} - \frac{\pi/2 - u}{\cos^2u} = \frac{G(2u)}{\sin^2u\cos^2u}, \\
G(v) := \frac32\sin v - \frac v2\cos v - \frac\pi4(1 - \cos v),
\end{gather*}
because $3\sin u\cos u = \tfrac32\sin 2u$ and $-u\cos^2u - (\pi/2 - u)\sin^2u = -u\cos 2u - \tfrac\pi4(1 - \cos 2u)$. Now $G(0) = 0$, $G'(v) = \cos v + (v/2 - \pi/4)\sin v$ with $G'(\pi/2) = 0$, and $G''(v) = -\tfrac12\sin v + (v/2 - \pi/4)\cos v < 0$ on $(0,\pi/2)$; hence $G' > 0$ and $G > 0$ on $(0,\pi/2)$, so $F' > 0$ on $(0,\pi/4)$, $F < F(\pi/4) = 0$ there, and $D'' < 0$ on $(0,\pi/2)$. A continuous function that is strictly concave on $(0,\pi/2)$ and vanishes at both ends of $[0,\pi/2]$ is positive inside, which proves $D > 0$ and the proposition.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $k \ge 1$, integration by parts with $h'(t) = \tfrac12\cot(t/2)$ gives
\[
\int_0^\pi h(t)\cos kt\,dt = -\frac1{2k}\int_0^\pi\cot(t/2)\sin kt\,dt = -\frac{\pi}{2k} :
\]
the boundary terms vanish because $h(t)\sin kt \to 0$ as $t \to 0$ and $\sin k\pi = 0$, and the last integral equals $\pi$ by the identity $\cot(t/2)\sin kt = 1 + \cos kt + 2\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\cos jt$. Since also $\int_0^\pi h = 0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cl2}(i), the even function $h \in L^2(-\pi,\pi)$ has the Fourier series $-\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-1}\cos kt$. For fixed $\vartheta$ let $g := \log|\cos\vartheta - \cos\cdot| \in L^2(0,\pi)$. By \eqref{eq:kernel_split}, the substitution $\varphi \mapsto -\varphi$ in the term $h(\vartheta - \varphi)$ and the periodicity of $h$, $\hat g_k = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}h(\vartheta+\varphi)\cos k\varphi\,d\varphi = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}h(t)\cos k(t-\vartheta)\,dt = -(\pi/k)\cos k\vartheta$ for $k \ge 1$, and $\hat g_0 = -\pi\log 2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cl2}(iv). Parseval's identity $\int_0^\pi gf = \pi^{-1}\hat g_0\hat f_0 + 2\pi^{-1}\sum_{k\ge1}\hat g_k\hat f_k$ gives the first identity of \eqref{eq:cheb}. By Bessel's inequality $\sum_{k\ge1}\hat f_k^{\,2} \le (\pi/2)\lVertf\rVert_{L^2}^2$, so $\sum_k k^{-1}|\hat f_k| \le (\pi^3/12)^{1/2}\lVertf\rVert_{L^2}$; the series therefore converges absolutely and uniformly, and integrating it termwise against $-f$ gives the second identity. Being uniformly convergent, the series is the cosine series of $E_f$, whose coefficients $-\pi\hat f_0\log 2$ and $-(\pi/k)\hat f_k$ determine $f$ by the completeness of $\{\cos k\varphi\}_{k\ge0}$ in $L^2(0,\pi)$; the same completeness gives $J_0(f) > 0$ when $\hat f_0 = 0 \ne f$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:minimum}
Let $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ be finite positive Borel measures with compact supports in $\mathbb R$ such that $\mu_2(\mathbb R) \le \mu_1(\mathbb R)$ and $U^{\mu_1}$ is continuous on $\mathbb C$, and let $K \subset \mathbb R$ be a nonempty compact set such that the positive part of $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ is carried by $K$. If $c \in \mathbb R$ and $u := U^{\mu_2} - U^{\mu_1} \ge c$ on $K$, then $u \ge c$ on $\mathbb C$. If moreover $u(z_0) = c$ at some $z_0 \in \mathbb C \setminus K$, then $c = 0$, $\mu_1(\mathbb R) = \mu_2(\mathbb R)$ and $u = 0$ on $\mathbb C\setminus K$.

name: A Minimum Principle for Potentials

title: Proof
body_md:
The potential of a finite positive measure with compact support is superharmonic on $\mathbb C$ and harmonic outside its support \cite[Thm.~3.1.2]{ransford1995potential}. Since $\mu_2 - \mu_1 = (\mu_2 - \mu_1)^+ - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)^+$ and the second measure is carried by $K$, the function $u$ is superharmonic on $D := \mathbb C\setminus K$, which is connected because $K \subset \mathbb R$, and $u$ is lower semicontinuous on $\mathbb C$ with values in $(-\infty,\infty]$. Let $R_0$ exceed the moduli of the points of both supports. For $|z| > R_0$, $u(z) = (\mu_1(\mathbb R) - \mu_2(\mathbb R))\log|z| + H(1/z)$ with $H(\zeta) := \mathrm{Re}\int\log(1 - s\zeta)\,d(\mu_1-\mu_2)(s)$, a harmonic function on $|\zeta| < 1/R_0$ with $H(0) = 0$.

Suppose that $m := \inf_{\mathbb C}u < c$. The infimum of $u$ over a closed disc is attained, since $u$ is lower semicontinuous. If $\mu_1(\mathbb R) > \mu_2(\mathbb R)$, then $u \to +\infty$ as $z \to \infty$, and $m$ is attained. If the masses are equal and $m$ is not attained, then $m = \lim_{z\to\infty}u(z) = 0 = H(0)$, so $H \ge H(0)$ near $0$; by the maximum principle for the subharmonic function $-H$ \cite[Thm.~2.3.1]{ransford1995potential}, $H$ vanishes near $0$, and $m$ is attained after all. In either case $m$ is attained at a point of $D$, since $u \ge c > m$ on $K$, and the maximum principle for $-u$ on $D$ shows that $u = m$ on $D$. This is impossible if $\mu_1(\mathbb R) > \mu_2(\mathbb R)$; if the masses are equal, it gives $m = \lim_{z\to\infty}u(z) = 0$, and, $D$ being dense in $\mathbb C$, the lower semicontinuity of $u$ gives $u \le 0 < c$ on $K$, a contradiction. Hence $u \ge c$ on $\mathbb C$. If $u(z_0) = c$ with $z_0 \in D$, then $u$ attains its infimum over $D$ at $z_0$, so $u = c$ on $D$; as above this forces $\mu_1(\mathbb R) = \mu_2(\mathbb R)$ and $c = 0$.

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Symmetry and counting.} The layer nodes come in pairs $\theta_m \leftrightarrow \pi - \theta_m = \theta_{N+1-m}$ with $\theta_m < \pi/2$, because $\theta_s < \pi/2$; each lattice in (ii) is symmetric by construction and, having an even number of points, does not contain $\pi/2$. Hence the multiset $Z_N$ without the point of (iii) is symmetric with multiplicities and has an even number of points, so $|Z_N| \equiv N - 1 \pmod 2$, and $P_N(-z) = \prod_{\zeta\in Z_N}(-1)\bigl(z - \cos(\pi-\zeta)\bigr) = (-1)^{|Z_N|}P_N(z)$ because $\cos(\pi - \zeta) = -\cos\zeta$ and $\zeta \mapsto \pi - \zeta$ permutes the multiset. The layer contains at most $2(\theta_s - \theta_0)N/\omega + 2$ nodes, and the smallest even integer with $K_k - 1 \ge x$ is less than $x + 3$, so $|Z_N| \le m(\mathcal C)N + 6Q + 3$, which is at most $N-1$ once $N(1 - m(\mathcal C)) \ge 6Q + 4$.

\emph{Potential estimates.} We have $\log|P_N(\cos\vartheta)| = \sum_{\zeta\in Z_N}g_\vartheta(\zeta)$. The layer nodes in $S$ are $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_q$ with $\theta_q \le \theta_s < \theta_q + \Delta$, and $q \ge 2$ once $\Delta \le \theta_s - \theta_0$. If $\vartheta$ is at distance at least $\Delta/4$ from them, Lemma~\ref{lem:riemann_arc} with $[\alpha,\beta] = [\theta_0, \theta_q] \subset [\xi, \pi - \xi]$, $K = q$ and $d = \Delta \le \xi/4 = \min\{\xi,1\}/4$ (which holds for $N \ge N_0$, as $\xi < 1$) gives
\[
\sum_{m=1}^q g_\vartheta(\theta_m) = \frac1\Delta\int_{\theta_0}^{\theta_q}g_\vartheta + O(\log N) = \frac N\omega\int_{\theta_0}^{\theta_s}g_\vartheta + O(\log N),
\]
since $1/\Delta = (N-1)/\omega$, $|\int_{\theta_0}^{\theta_s}g_\vartheta| \le C$, and $|\int_{\theta_q}^{\theta_s}g_\vartheta| \le C\Delta\log(1/\Delta)$ by the estimate of the end half-cells in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:riemann}, $[\theta_q, \theta_s]$ being an interval of length at most $\Delta$ inside $[\xi/2, \pi - \xi/2]$. The mirror layer is treated in the same way. For the $k$-th lattice on an arc $[\alpha,\beta]$ (one of $A_k$, $\pi - A_k$, or $A_k^\ast$), Lemma~\ref{lem:riemann_arc} with $d = d_k \le 1/(\rho_kN) \le \min\{\xi,1\}/4$ (for $N \ge N_0$) gives $\sum_ig_\vartheta(\varphi_i^{(k)}) = d_k^{-1}\int_\alpha^\beta g_\vartheta + O(\log N)$ when $\vartheta$ is at distance at least $d_k/4$ from its points, and $d_k^{-1} = (K_k-1)/(\beta - \alpha) \in [\rho_kN, \rho_kN + 2/(\beta-\alpha))$ together with $|\int_\alpha^\beta g_\vartheta| \le C$ gives $d_k^{-1}\int_\alpha^\beta g_\vartheta = \rho_kN\int_\alpha^\beta g_\vartheta + O(1)$. Adding the finitely many lattices and, for even $N$, the term $g_\vartheta(\pi/2) = \log|\cos\vartheta|$, we obtain
\[
\log|P_N(\cos\vartheta)| = NE(\vartheta) + O(\log N) + \begin{cases}\log|\cos\vartheta|, & N \text{ even},\\ 0, & N \text{ odd},\end{cases}
\]
under the hypotheses of (b); there $|\cos\vartheta| = |\sin(\vartheta - \pi/2)| \ge 2/(\pi N)$ by the first elementary fact, since $1/N \le |\vartheta - \pi/2| \le \pi/2$, which proves (b). For (a), each lattice contains at most one point within a quarter spacing of $\vartheta$, its points being one spacing apart; omitting these points, whose factors satisfy $g_\vartheta(\zeta) \le \log 2$, and using case (b) of Lemma~\ref{lem:riemann_arc} for the lattices concerned and $\log|\cos\vartheta| \le 0$ gives the upper bound.

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) $\ell_1^V$ and $\ell_N^V$ vanish at the interior nodes by definition. By the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:unisolvence}, $R$ maps $V_N$ onto itself and permutes the nodes, $x_{N+1-m} = L - x_m$, so $R\ell_1^V$ is the Lagrange function of $V_N$ at $x_N$: $R\ell_1^V = \ell_N^V$, $R\ell_N^V = \ell_1^V$, and $R\chi_N^{\pm} = \ell_N^V \pm \ell_1^V = \pm \chi_N^{\pm}$.

(ii) By Proposition~\ref{prop:lagrange_norms} with $m = 1$ and $z_1 = c_0$, $\lVert\ell_1^V\rVert_{L^\infty(I)} \le \exp(C\log N)$ and $\lVert\ell_1^V\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)} \le \exp\bigl(N[U_\omega(c_0) - U_\omega(1)] + C\log N\bigr)$, and $U_\omega(c_0) - U_\omega(1) = \kappa_\sigma - \kappa_\Lambda$ by \eqref{eq:rates}; the same bounds hold for $\ell_N^V = R\ell_1^V$, and the triangle inequality gives (ii).

(iii) \emph{Sign structure.} By the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:lagrange_norms}, $\ell_1^V(x) = (\sin\vartheta/\sin\theta_0)\,\ell_1(\cos\vartheta)$ and $\ell_N^V(x) = (\sin\vartheta/\sin\theta_0)\,\ell_N(\cos\vartheta)$ with $\vartheta = \pi(x+\delta)/\tilde L$, since $\sin\theta_N = \sin\theta_0$. The two Lagrange polynomials are related by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lagrange_mirror}
(-1)^{N-1}(z + c_0)\,\ell_N(z) = (z - c_0)\,\ell_1(z):
\end{equation}
indeed $\ell_N(z)/\ell_1(z) = \frac{z - z_1}{z - z_N}\prod_{k\ge2}(z_1 - z_k)\big/\prod_{k\le N-1}(z_N - z_k)$, and since $z_N = -c_0$ and $z_{N+1-k} = -z_k$, $\prod_{k\le N-1}(z_N - z_k) = (-1)^{N-1}\prod_{k\le N-1}(c_0 + z_k) = (-1)^{N-1}\prod_{k\ge2}(c_0 - z_k)$, so that $\ell_N(z) = (-1)^{N-1}\frac{z - c_0}{z + c_0}\,\ell_1(z)$. For $x \in (-\delta, 0)$, i.e.\ $\vartheta \in (0,\theta_0)$ and $z = \cos\vartheta \in (c_0, 1)$, every factor of $\ell_1(z) = \prod_{k\ge2}(z - z_k)/(z_1 - z_k)$ is positive, so $\ell_1^V(x) > 0$, and $0 < (z - c_0)/(z + c_0) < 1$; by \eqref{eq:lagrange_mirror},
\[
\chi_N^{\pm} = \ell_1^V\Bigl(1 \pm (-1)^{N-1}\frac{z - c_0}{z + c_0}\Bigr) \ge \frac{2c_0}{1 + c_0}\,\ell_1^V > 0 \quad\text{on } (-\delta, 0),
\]
because $1 + (z-c_0)/(z+c_0) = 2z/(z+c_0) \ge 1$ and $1 - (z-c_0)/(z+c_0) = 2c_0/(z+c_0) \ge 2c_0/(1+c_0)$ for $z \in (c_0,1)$; and $\chi_N^{\pm}(L - x) = \pm \chi_N^{\pm}(x)$ by (i).

\emph{Lower bound.} Split $p_N^{\pm}$ into the integrals over $(-\delta,0)$, $(L, L+\delta)$ and $I$. By (ii) and $0 \le \tilde G(0,y) \le \delta(L+\delta)/\tilde L$, the integral over $I$ is at most $N^C$ in modulus. In the integral over $(L,L+\delta)$ substitute $y = L - y'$ and use the symmetry of $\chi_N^{\pm}$; with $\tilde G(0,y') = (y'+\delta)(L+\delta)/\tilde L$ and $\tilde G(0, L-y') = \delta(y'+\delta)/\tilde L$ for $y' \in (-\delta,0)$, which follow from the formula for $\tilde G$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:unisolvence}, the two extension integrals add up to
\[
\int_{-\delta}^0\frac{(L+\delta) \pm \delta}{\tilde L}\,(y'+\delta)\,\chi_N^{\pm}(y')\,dy' \ \ge\ \frac{L}{\tilde L}\int_{-\delta}^0(y'+\delta)\,\chi_N^{\pm}(y')\,dy' ,
\]
since $\chi_N^{\pm} > 0$ there and $(L+\delta) \pm \delta \ge L$. Restrict the last integral to the $y'$ with $\vartheta = \pi(y'+\delta)/\tilde L \in [1/N, 2/N]$, an interval of length $\tilde L/(\pi N)$ on which $y' + \delta \ge \tilde L/(\pi N)$. For $N \ge N_0$ such $\vartheta$ is at distance at least $\Delta/4$ from every node, so Lemma~\ref{lem:lagrange_polynomials}(b) and Lemma~\ref{lem:U_modulus} give $|\ell_1(\cos\vartheta)| \ge \exp\bigl(N[U_\omega(c_0) - U_\omega(\cos\vartheta)] - C\log N\bigr) \ge \exp\bigl(N[U_\omega(c_0) - U_\omega(1)] - C\log N\bigr)$, and $\sin\vartheta \ge 2/(\pi N)$; hence $\chi_N^{\pm} \ge c_0\,\ell_1^V \ge \exp\bigl(N(\kappa_\sigma-\kappa_\Lambda) - C\log N\bigr)$ there. Collecting the factors, $p_N^{\pm} \ge \exp\bigl(N(\kappa_\sigma-\kappa_\Lambda) - C\log N\bigr) - N^C$, which gives (iii) for $N \ge N_0$ because $\kappa_\sigma > \kappa_\Lambda$.

\emph{Consequence.} By the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:unisolvence}, $\psi \in V_N$ lies in $\Psi_N$ if and only if $v := \tilde\mathcal{L}_P^{-1}\psi$ vanishes at $0$ and at $L$, and $v(0) = \int_{\tilde I}\tilde G(0,y)\psi(y)\,dy$. Since $R$ commutes with $\tilde\mathcal{L}_P^{-1}$ on $V_N$ and $Rg = \pm g$, one has $v(L) = \pm v(0)$ for $v = \tilde\mathcal{L}_P^{-1}g$, and $v(0) = (\tilde\mathcal{L}_P^{-1}g_0)(0) - \alpha p_N^{\pm} = 0$ by the choice of $\alpha$; so $g \in \Psi_N$. The nodal values are those of $g_0$ by (i), and \eqref{eq:alpha_bound} follows from $|(\tilde\mathcal{L}_P^{-1}g_0)(0)| \le \lVert\tilde G(0,\cdot)\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)}\lVertg_0\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)}$ and (iii).

Let $Z_N$ and $P_N$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:construction} and $g_0 := \sin\theta\,P_N(\cos\theta)$, a function of $V_N$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:chebyshev_variable} since $|Z_N| \le N-1$. Under $R$, $\theta \mapsto \pi - \theta$, $\sin\theta$ is invariant and $z \mapsto -z$, so $Rg_0 = (-1)^{N-1}g_0$ by the symmetry of $P_N$. Lemma~\ref{lem:correction}, with the sign $\pm = (-1)^{N-1}$ of $g_0$, gives $g := g_0 - \alpha\chi_N^{\pm} \in \Psi_N$; put $v := \tilde\mathcal{L}_P^{-1}g \in \Phi_N$ and let $\mathbf{w}_N$ be its coefficient vector, $v = \Phi\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w}_N$, which exists and is unique because $\{\varphi_j\}$ is a basis of $\Phi_N$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:dimensions}). Since $(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w}_N)_m = (\mathcal{L}_Pv)(x_m) = g(x_m)$, the vector $\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}_N$ consists of the values of $g$, i.e.\ of $g_0$, at the interior nodes.

\emph{Nodal values.} At the layer nodes $g_0$ vanishes. Every other interior node satisfies $\theta_m \in (\theta_s, \pi - \theta_s)$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:construction}(a) gives $|g_0(x_m)| \le |P_N(\cos\theta_m)| \le \exp(NE_c + C\log N)$, and $\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}_N\rVert_2 \le \exp(NE_c + C\log N)$.

\emph{Coefficient norm.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:construction}(a), $|g_0| \le \exp(NE_{\max} + C\log N)$ on $\tilde I$, hence $\lVertg_0\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)} \le \exp(NE_{\max} + C\log N)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:correction}(ii) and \eqref{eq:alpha_bound}, $|\alpha|\lVert\chi_N^{\pm}\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)} \le N^C\lVertg_0\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)}$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:coefficient_norm} gives $\lVert\mathbf{w}_N\rVert_2 \le C_B\sqrt N\bigl(\lVertg_0\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)} + |\alpha|\lVert\chi_N^{\pm}\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)}\bigr) \le \exp(NE_{\max} + C\log N)$.

\emph{Size on $I$.} Let $[x_a,x_b]$ be the image of $[\theta_0 + \Delta/4, \theta_0 + 3\Delta/4]$ under $x = \tilde L\theta/\pi - \delta$, an interval of length $h_b = \tilde L\Delta/(2\pi)$ inside $I$, between the layer nodes $\theta_1 = \theta_0$ and $\theta_2 = \theta_0 + \Delta$ (both lie in $S$ for $N \ge N_0$). Its points are at distance at least $\Delta/4$ from every node, at distance at least $\theta_0 - \max_k\beta_k > 0$ (maximum over the extension arcs, if there are any) from every extension lattice, and at distance at least $\theta_s - \theta_0 - \Delta$ from every centre lattice and from $\pi/2$; for $N \ge N_0$ these distances exceed the respective quarter spacings and $1/N$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:construction}(b) applies, and with \eqref{eq:E_modulus} for $|\vartheta - \theta_0| \le 3\Delta/4$ it gives $|P_N(\cos\vartheta)| \ge \exp\bigl(NE(\vartheta) - C\log N\bigr) \ge \exp\bigl(NE(\theta_0) - C\log N\bigr)$ on $[x_a,x_b]$. No point of $Z_N$ lies in $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$, so $P_N(\cos\theta)$ has constant sign on $[x_a, x_b]$, and so has $g_0$, with $|g_0| \ge \sin\theta_0\exp\bigl(NE(\theta_0) - C\log N\bigr) =: 2g_\ast$. On $I$ the correction satisfies $|\alpha\chi_N^{\pm}| \le \exp\bigl(N(E_{\max} - (\kappa_\sigma - \kappa_\Lambda)) + C\log N\bigr)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:correction}(ii) and \eqref{eq:alpha_bound}, which is at most $g_\ast$ for $N \ge N_0$ because $E(\theta_0) - E_{\max} = \ell > -(\kappa_\sigma - \kappa_\Lambda)$. Hence $g = g_0 - \alpha\chi_N^{\pm}$ has the sign of $g_0$ and $|g| \ge g_\ast$ on $[x_a,x_b]$. As $v \in \Phi_N$ is smooth with $-v'' = \mathcal{L}_Pv = g$ on $\tilde I$, Lemma~\ref{lem:bump} gives $\lVertv\rVert_{L^2(I)} \ge g_\ast h_b^{5/2}/(32\pi^2) \ge \exp\bigl(NE(\theta_0) - C\log N\bigr)$; in particular $v \ne 0$ and $\mathbf{w}_N \ne 0$.

\emph{Conclusion.} For $s \in [0,1]$ the three estimates give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log\frac{\lVert\Phi\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w}_N\rVert_{L^2(I)}}{\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}_N\rVert_2^{\,s}\lVert\mathbf{w}_N\rVert_2^{\,1-s}} &\ge N\bigl[E(\theta_0) - sE_c - (1-s)E_{\max}\bigr] - C\log N \\
&= N(\ell + s\tau) - C\log N,
\end{aligned}
\]
since $E(\theta_0) - sE_c - (1-s)E_{\max} = (E(\theta_0) - E_{\max}) + s(E_{\max} - E_c)$.

body_md:
(i) Let $t > 0$ and $\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal V_t^\perp\setminus\{0\}$, and for $k \ge 0$ let $\mathbf{w}_k$ be the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{w}$ onto the span of the $\mathbf{v}_i$ with $t2^k < \sigma_i \le t2^{k+1}$, so that $\mathbf{w} = \sum_k\mathbf{w}_k$, a finite sum. Since $\mathbf{w}_k \in \mathcal V_{t2^{k+1}}$, $\lVert\Phi\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w}_k\rVert_{L^2(I)} \le C(t2^{k+1})^b\lVert\mathbf{w}_k\rVert_2$, and $\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}_k\rVert_2 \ge t2^k\lVert\mathbf{w}_k\rVert_2$; the vectors $\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}_k$ are pairwise orthogonal, as they lie in the spans of disjoint sets of left singular vectors. By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and $\sum_{k\ge0}4^{k(b-1)} = (1 - 4^{b-1})^{-1}$,
\[
\lVert\Phi\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w}\rVert_{L^2(I)} \le \sum_kC2^b(t2^k)^{b-1}\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}_k\rVert_2 \le C_bt^{b-1}\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 .
\]
(ii) Let $\mathbf{w} \ne 0$; then $\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w} \ne 0$ because $\mathbf{B}_D$ is nonsingular under Assumption~\ref{ass:unisolvence}. Split $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w}_t + \mathbf{w}_t^\perp$ as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:two_constant}. Since $\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}_t$ and $\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}_t^\perp$ are orthogonal, $\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}_t^\perp\rVert_2 \le \lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2$, so $\lVert\Phi\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w}\rVert_{L^2(I)} \le \gamma_t\lVert\mathbf{w}_t\rVert_2 + \Gamma_t\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}_t^\perp\rVert_2 \le Ct^b\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 + C't^{b-1}\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2$, and $t := \lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2$ gives the first claim. The converse is immediate from the definitions \eqref{eq:two_constants}, since $\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \le t\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2$ on $\mathcal V_t$ and $\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \le \lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2/t$ on $\mathcal V_t^\perp$.

label: eq:dual_core
title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Reduction.} We show that for $N \ge N_0$, every $t \ge 0$ and every $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb R^n$ with $\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \le 1$ and $\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \le t$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dual_core}
\lVert\Phi\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w}\rVert_{L^2(I)} \le N^C\bigl(t\,e^{NA_1(\mathcal S)} + e^{NA_2(\mathcal S)}\bigr).
\end{equation}
This gives \eqref{eq:dual_bound}: a unit vector $\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal V_t$ satisfies $\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \le t$, so $\gamma_t$ is at most the right-hand side; and for $\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal V_t^\perp\setminus\{0\}$ and $t > 0$ one has $\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \ge t\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 > 0$, as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:apriori}, so $\mathbf{w}' := t\mathbf{w}/\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2$ satisfies $\lVert\mathbf{w}'\rVert_2 \le 1$ and $\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}'\rVert_2 = t$, and \eqref{eq:dual_core} for $\mathbf{w}'$ reads $t\lVert\Phi\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w}\rVert_{L^2(I)}/\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \le N^C(te^{NA_1(\mathcal S)} + e^{NA_2(\mathcal S)})$, whence the bound on $t\Gamma_t$; for $t = 0$ the term $t\Gamma_t$ vanishes. Estimate \eqref{eq:dual_rate} follows from \eqref{eq:dual_bound} with $t = e^{-N\tau}$, since then $te^{NA_1(\mathcal S)} + e^{NA_2(\mathcal S)} \le 2e^{N\Phi(\mathcal S,\tau)}$.

\emph{Norms.} Let $\mathbf{w}$ be as in \eqref{eq:dual_core}, $v := \Phi\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w} \in \Phi_N$ and $\psi := \mathcal{L} v \in \Psi_N \subset V_N$. Since $v \in C^2(\bar I)$ vanishes at $0$ and $L$ and $\mathcal{L} v = \psi$, Lemma~\ref{lem:dirichlet_box}(iii) with $d = 1$ gives $\lVertv\rVert_{L^2(I)} \le (L/\pi)^2\lVert\psi\rVert_{L^2(I)} \le (L/\pi)^2\sqrt L\,\lVert\psi\rVert_{L^\infty(I)}$. The values of $\psi$ at the interior nodes are the entries of $\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}$, so $|\psi(x_m)| \le t$ for $2 \le m \le N-1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:test_norm}, $\lVert\psi\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)} \le C_\Psi\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2/\sqrt N \le C_\Psi/\sqrt N$, and since $\psi = \sum_{j=1}^Nc_jw_j$ with $\sum_jc_j^2 = \lVert\psi\rVert^2_{L^2(\tilde I)}$ and $|w_j| \le \sqrt{2/\tilde L}$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives $|\psi(x)| \le \sqrt{2N/\tilde L}\,\lVert\psi\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)} \le C$ for all $x \in \tilde I$.

\emph{Interpolation.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:chebyshev_variable}, $\psi(x) = \sin\theta\,p(\cos\theta)$ with $p \in \mathbb P_{N-1}$ and $\theta = \pi(x+\delta)/\tilde L$. At a node $s = \theta_m$ of $S_N$, which is an interior node, $|p(\cos s)| = |\psi(x_m)|/\sin\theta_m \le t/\sin\theta_0$; at a point $s$ of a virtual lattice, $s \in [\xi,\pi-\xi]$ and $|p(\cos s)| = |\psi(x)|/\sin s \le C/\sin\xi$. Since $S_N$ consists of $N' \ge N$ distinct points and $\deg p \le N-1 \le N'-1$, Lagrange interpolation reproduces $p$: $p = \sum_{s\in S_N}p(\cos s)\,\ell_s$. For $\vartheta \in [\theta_0,\pi-\theta_0]$ we have $E(\vartheta) \le E_I$, and $E(s) \ge E_1$ for the nodes of $S_N$ and $E(s) \ge E_2$ for the virtual points, because the former lie in the node arcs and the latter in the virtual arcs; so \eqref{eq:lattice_lagrange} gives $|\ell_s(\cos\vartheta)| \le N^Ce^{NA_1(\mathcal S)}$ for the nodes and $|\ell_s(\cos\vartheta)| \le N^Ce^{NA_2(\mathcal S)}$ for the virtual points. Summing the $N' \le N + C$ terms,
\[
|\psi(x)| \le |p(\cos\vartheta)| \le N^C\Bigl(\frac{t}{\sin\theta_0}\,e^{NA_1(\mathcal S)} + \frac{C}{\sin\xi}\,e^{NA_2(\mathcal S)}\Bigr), \qquad x \in \bar I,\ \vartheta = \pi(x+\delta)/\tilde L,
\]
and the bound on $\lVertv\rVert_{L^2(I)}$ of the previous step gives \eqref{eq:dual_core}.

body_md:
\emph{Monotonicity and the Lipschitz bound.} Let $0 < \tau \le \tau' < \kappa_\sigma$. A triple that is admissible in \eqref{eq:reduced_problem} at the level $\tau'$ is admissible at the level $\tau$; and if $(F, b, \nu)$ is admissible at the level $\tau$, then $(F, b - (\tau' - \tau), \nu)$ is admissible at the level $\tau'$, with a value smaller by $\tau' - \tau$. Hence $m_\omega(\tau') \le m_\omega(\tau) \le m_\omega(\tau') + \tau' - \tau$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:extremal} gives the same inequalities for $r_\omega$.

\emph{The bounds.} Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(i) gives $-\tau \le r_\omega(\tau) \le 0$. Below, $\lambda := \lambda_\tau$ and $\mu_\omega$ are identified with their images on $[-1,1]$; both potentials are continuous by Lemma~\ref{lem:env}(d), and $U^{\mu_\omega} = U_\omega$. For the upper bound $\kappa_\Lambda - \tau$ let $K'$ be the image of the support of $(\omega^{-1}d\theta - \lambda)|_{\Theta_I}$; it is nonempty because $\lambda(\Theta_I) < 1$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(iii), and it carries the positive part of $\mu_\omega - \lambda$, the image of $(\omega^{-1}d\theta - \lambda)|_{\Theta_I}$. On $K'$, $E_\tau = E_\tau^\ast - \tau$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(ii) and $U_\omega \le U_\omega(0)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:clausen}, so that $u := U^\lambda - U_\omega = -E_\tau - U_\omega \ge \tau - E_\tau^\ast - U_\omega(0)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:minimum} with $(\mu_1,\mu_2) = (\mu_\omega,\lambda)$, whose masses are equal, extends this to $\mathbb C$; at $c_0$ it reads $r_\omega(\tau) = E_\tau(\theta_0) - E_\tau^\ast \le U_\omega(0) - U_\omega(c_0) - \tau = \kappa_\Lambda - \tau$ by \eqref{eq:rates}.

For the strict lower bound let $K$ be the support of $\lambda|_{\Theta_E}$, nonempty by Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(iii), and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:minimum} with $(\mu_1,\mu_2) = (\lambda,\mu_\omega)$: the masses are equal, and the positive part of $\lambda - \mu_\omega$ is carried by $K$ because $\lambda \le \mu_\omega$ on $\Theta_I$. On $K$, $u := U^{\mu_\omega} - U^\lambda = U_\omega + E_\tau \ge U_\omega(1) + E_\tau^\ast$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(ii) and Lemma~\ref{lem:clausen}. Hence $u \ge U_\omega(1) + E_\tau^\ast$ on $\mathbb C$, and at $c_0$ this reads $r_\omega(\tau) = E_\tau(\theta_0) - E_\tau^\ast \ge U_\omega(1) - U_\omega(c_0) = \kappa_\Lambda - \kappa_\sigma$ by \eqref{eq:rates}. name: Discretization of the Equilibrium Measure

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\lambda := \lambda_\tau = f\,d\theta$, $E := E_\tau$, $E^\ast := E_\tau^\ast$, and $\theta_\tau$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(iii). For $0 < \eta \le \theta_0/2$ with $\eta < \min\{1/4, \omega/2\}$ let $\mathcal P$ be a partition of $[0,\pi]$ into arcs with pairwise disjoint interiors and lengths in $[\eta/2,\eta]$, invariant under $\vartheta \mapsto \pi - \vartheta$, of which $\theta_0$, $\pi/2$ and $\pi - \theta_0$ are endpoints; it exists because $[0,\theta_0]$ and $[\theta_0,\pi/2]$ have lengths at least $\eta$. For $A \in \mathcal P$ put $f_A := \lambda(A)/|A| \le 1/\omega$, and let $\bar\lambda$ have density $f_A$ on each $A \in \mathcal P$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:env}, $|E_{\bar\lambda} - E| \le 8\omega^{-1}\Omega(\eta)$ on $[0,\pi]$, $|E(\vartheta) - E(\vartheta')| \le \omega^{-1}\Omega(\eta)$ for $|\vartheta - \vartheta'| \le \eta$, and $|E_g| \le MC_0|B|^{1/2}$ on $[0,\pi]$ for every $g$ with $|g| \le M$ that vanishes outside a Borel set $B$. Below, $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \dots$ denote quantities that depend only on $\eta$, $\omega$ and $\tau$ and tend to $0$ as $\eta \to 0$.

\emph{The configuration.} The set $K := \{\vartheta \in [\theta_0,\pi/2] : E(\vartheta) + \tau \ge E^\ast + \varepsilon/4\}$ is compact and, as $E + \tau = E^\ast$ on $[\theta_\tau,\pi/2]$, contained in $[\theta_0,\theta_\tau)$. If $\theta_\tau > \theta_0$, let $\eta$ be so small that some endpoint $\theta_s$ of $\mathcal P$ satisfies $\max(K \cup\{\theta_0\}) < \theta_s < \theta_\tau$; if $\theta_\tau = \theta_0$, let $\theta_s$ be the endpoint of $\mathcal P$ next to $\theta_0$ on its right. Let $\xi \le \eta$ be the smallest positive endpoint and $\theta_0 - \zeta$, $\zeta \le \eta$, the endpoint next to $\theta_0$ on its left. The configuration $\mathcal C$ has the layer parameter $\theta_s$, the extension arcs $A \in \mathcal P$ with $A \subset [\xi,\theta_0-\zeta]$ and $f_A > 0$, the centre arcs $A \in \mathcal P$ with $A \subset [\theta_s,\pi/2]$ and $f_A > 0$, and on these arcs the densities $(1 - \eta')f_A$ with $\eta' := \eta(1 + 2/\omega)$; for $\eta' < 1$ it satisfies Definition~\ref{def:configuration}, its total mass being at most $\max\{\lambda(S^\ast) + (1-\eta')(1 - \lambda(S^\ast)),\ 2\eta/\omega + 1 - \eta'\} < 1$. Its envelope is $E_\nu$ for the measure $\nu$ of density $1/\omega$ on $S^\ast$ and $(1-\eta')f_A$ on the arcs. The density of $\nu - \bar\lambda$ vanishes on the layer if $\theta_s < \theta_\tau$, where $f = 1/\omega$, is bounded by $1/\omega$ on the layer if $\theta_\tau = \theta_0$, where $|S^\ast| \le 2\eta$, and on $[0,\xi) \cup (\theta_0 - \zeta,\theta_0)$ and its mirror image, of measure at most $4\eta$, and is bounded by $\eta'/\omega$ elsewhere. Hence $|E_\nu - E| \le \varepsilon_1 := 8\omega^{-1}\Omega(\eta) + \omega^{-1}C_0\bigl((6\eta)^{1/2} + \eta'\sqrt\pi\bigr)$ on $[0,\pi]$. Since $E^\ast = \max E$, $E \le E^\ast - \tau + \varepsilon/4$ on $[\theta_s,\pi-\theta_s]$ and $E(\theta_0) - E^\ast = r_\omega(\tau)$, this gives $\tau(\mathcal C) \ge \tau - \varepsilon/4 - 2\varepsilon_1$ and $\ell(\mathcal C) \ge r_\omega(\tau) - 2\varepsilon_1$, and $2\varepsilon_1 \le 3\varepsilon/4$ for small $\eta$.

\emph{The interpolation configuration.} Let $q \in \mathbb N$ with $q \ge 1/\eta$, and shrink every arc of $\mathcal P$ by $\eta^2$ at both ends. For each $A \in \mathcal P$ with $A \subset \Theta_I$ let $r_A := \lfloor(1-\eta)q\omega f_A\rfloor \in \{0,\dots,q-1\}$; the shrunk arcs with $r_A \ge 1$ are the node arcs, with modulus $q$, residues $\{0,\dots,r_A - 1\}$ and density $\rho_A = r_A/(q\omega) \in [(1-\eta)f_A - \eta/\omega,\ (1-\eta)f_A]$. There are node arcs for small $\eta$: by Lemma~\ref{lem:cheb}, $J_0(\lambda) \ge \log 2 = J_0(\pi^{-1}d\theta)$, and $J_\tau(\lambda) \le J_\tau(\pi^{-1}d\theta)$ then gives $\lambda(\Theta_I) \ge \omega/\pi$, so $f_A \ge 1/\pi$ for some $A \subset \Theta_I$, and $r_A \ge 1$ for this $A$ once $(1 - \eta)\omega \ge \pi\eta$. The shrunk arcs of the $A \in \mathcal P$ with $A \subset \overline{\Theta_E}\cap[\xi,\pi-\xi]$ and $f_A > 0$ are the virtual arcs, with density $(1 + \varkappa)f_A$, where $\varkappa \ge 0$ makes the total mass one. Since $\lambda(\Theta_E) > 0$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(iii), virtual arcs exist for small $\eta$ and $\varkappa \le \varepsilon_2$, because the mass removed by the floors, which lower the density by at most $2\eta/\omega$ on $\Theta_I$, by the shrinking, which removes at most $4\pi\eta$ of length, and with the arcs in $[0,\xi)\cup(\pi-\xi,\pi]$ is at most $2\eta + (4\pi + 2)\eta/\omega$, while the mass of $\lambda$ on the virtual arcs tends to $\lambda(\Theta_E)$. The arcs are pairwise disjoint, so $\mathcal S$ is an interpolation configuration, and as before its envelope satisfies $|E_{\mathcal S} - E| \le \varepsilon_3$ on $[0,\pi]$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(i), $E \ge E^\ast - \tau$ everywhere, so the minimum of $E_{\mathcal S}$ over the node arcs is at least $E^\ast - \tau - \varepsilon_3$. Every virtual arc lies in some $A \in \mathcal P$ with $A \subset \overline{\Theta_E}$ and $\lambda(A) > 0$, hence within $\eta$ of the support of $\lambda|_{\Theta_E}$, where $E = E^\ast$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(ii); so the minimum of $E_{\mathcal S}$ over the virtual arcs is at least $E^\ast - \omega^{-1}\Omega(\eta) - \varepsilon_3$. Finally $\max_{\Theta_I}E_{\mathcal S} \le E(\theta_0) + \varepsilon_3$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(iii). Therefore $A_1(\mathcal S) - \tau \le r_\omega(\tau) + 2\varepsilon_3$ and $A_2(\mathcal S) \le r_\omega(\tau) + 2\varepsilon_3 + \omega^{-1}\Omega(\eta)$, so that $\Phi(\mathcal S,\tau) \le r_\omega(\tau) + \varepsilon$ for small $\eta$.

Let $N \ge N_0$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:unisolvence_poisson}, so that $\mathbf{B}_D$ is nonsingular and $\mathcal V_0 = \{0\}$. For $t > 0$ and $\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal V_t$, $\lVert\Phi\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w}\rVert_{L^2(I)} \le \Gamma_0\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \le t\Gamma_0\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2$, and for $\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal V_t^\perp$, $\lVert\Phi\mathbf{D}\mathbf{w}\rVert_{L^2(I)} \le \Gamma_0\lVert\mathbf{B}_D\mathbf{w}\rVert_2$; hence $\max\{\gamma_t, t\Gamma_t\} \le t\Gamma_0$. For $\tau \in (0,\kappa_\sigma)$ and $t = t_N = e^{-N\tau}$, Theorem~\ref{thm:tail_law} therefore gives $\liminf_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\log\Gamma_0 \ge r_\omega(\tau) + \tau$, and letting $\tau \to \kappa_\sigma$, Proposition~\ref{prop:tail_properties} gives $\liminf_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\log\Gamma_0 \ge \kappa_\Lambda$. Conversely, Proposition~\ref{prop:classical}(i) with $t = 0$ and $\Lambda^\Psi_{N,2} \le \sqrt L\,\Lambda_N^\Psi$ give $\Gamma_0 \le (L^2/\pi^2)\sqrt{nL}\,\Lambda_N^\Psi$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:classical}(iii) gives $\Lambda_N^\Psi \le N^Ce^{N\kappa_\Lambda}$. Hence
\[
\kappa_\Lambda \le \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log\Gamma_0}{N} \le \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log\Lambda_N^\Psi}{N} \le \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log\Lambda_N^\Psi}{N} \le \kappa_\Lambda ,
\]
and $\limsup_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\log\Gamma_0 \le \limsup_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\log\Lambda_N^\Psi = \kappa_\Lambda$.

body_md: For symmetric $\lambda = f\,d\theta \in \mathscr A_\omega$ put $T\lambda := c\,(\omega^{-1} - \mathcal Rf)\,d\theta$. Its density lies in $[0,c/\omega] = [0,1/\omega']$, its mass is $c(\pi/\omega - 1) = 1$, and it is symmetric, so $T$ maps the symmetric elements of $\mathscr A_\omega$ onto those of $\mathscr A_{\omega'}$, the inverse being $\mu \mapsto \mathcal R(\omega^{-1} - c^{-1}\,d\mu/d\theta)\,d\theta$. The density of $T\lambda$ has the cosine coefficients $1$ and $-c\cos(k\pi/2)\hat f_k$, $k \ge 1$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:cheb} gives $J_0(T\lambda) = \log 2 + c^2(J_0(\lambda) - \log 2)$; moreover $(T\lambda)(\Theta_I') = c(\omega'/\omega - \lambda(\Theta_E)) = 1 - c + c\lambda(\Theta_I)$. Hence $J'_{c\tau}(T\lambda) = c^2J_\tau(\lambda) + (1 - c^2)\log 2 - 2c(1-c)\tau$ for symmetric $\lambda$, so $T\lambda_\tau$ minimizes $J'_{c\tau}$ over the symmetric elements of $\mathscr A_{\omega'}$; as the minimizer $\lambda'_{c\tau}$ of $J'_{c\tau}$ over $\mathscr A_{\omega'}$ is symmetric and unique (Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}), $T\lambda_\tau = \lambda'_{c\tau}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cl2}(iv), $E_{T\lambda}(\vartheta) = -c\bigl((\pi/\omega)\log 2 + E_\lambda(|\vartheta - \pi/2|)\bigr)$; with $\lambda = \lambda_\tau$ this gives $\max_{[0,\pi]}E_{T\lambda} = -c\bigl((\pi/\omega)\log 2 + \min_{[0,\pi]}E_\tau\bigr)$ and, as $|\theta_0' - \pi/2| = \theta_0$, $E_{T\lambda}(\theta_0') = -c\bigl((\pi/\omega)\log 2 + E_\tau(\theta_0)\bigr)$. Let $0 < \tau < \kappa_\sigma(\omega)$. Then $\min E_\tau = E_\tau^\ast - \tau$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:equilibrium}(i) and (iii), and $c\tau \in (0,\kappa_\sigma(\omega'))$ because $\omega\kappa_\sigma(\omega) = \mathrm{Cl}_2(\omega) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-\omega)$ is symmetric in $\omega$ and $\pi-\omega$. Therefore $r_{\omega'}(c\tau) = E_{T\lambda}(\theta_0') - \max E_{T\lambda} = c\bigl(\min E_\tau - E_\tau(\theta_0)\bigr) = -c\bigl(\tau + r_\omega(\tau)\bigr)$. Dividing by $c\kappa_\sigma(\omega) = \kappa_\sigma(\omega')$ gives \eqref{eq:tail_duality} at $\bar\tau = \tau/\kappa_\sigma(\omega)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{The profile.} Let $r_0 := \min\{\theta_0,\omega\}/4$, choose $x_\ast < -g$ with $m \ge 1/(2\pi)$ on $(-\infty,x_\ast]$, which is possible by Lemma~\ref{lem:inner}(iii), and let $0 < \tau \le \tau_1$, where $\tau_1 \in (0,\min\{1,\kappa_\sigma\})$ satisfies $2\tau_1(l - x_\ast) \le r_0$. Define on $[0,\pi]$
\[
e_\tau(\vartheta) := \frac\omega\pi + 1 + e\Bigl(\frac{\vartheta - \theta_0}{\tau}\Bigr) + e\Bigl(\frac{\pi - \theta_0 - \vartheta}{\tau}\Bigr).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:inner}(i), $e_\tau$ is absolutely continuous, $e_\tau' \in L^2(0,\pi)$, and $e_\tau'$ is H\"older continuous near every point of $(0,\pi)\setminus\{\theta_0,\pi-\theta_0\}$. Since $-1 \le e \le 0$, $e = 0$ on $(-\infty,-g]$ and $e = -1$ on $[l,\infty)$, and since $(\pi - \theta_0 - \vartheta)/\tau \ge \omega/(2\tau) \ge l$ for $\vartheta \le \pi/2$, we have $e_\tau(\pi - \vartheta) = e_\tau(\vartheta)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:profile}
e_\tau \le \frac\omega\pi \ \text{ on } [0,\pi], \qquad e_\tau = \frac\omega\pi - 1 \ \text{ on } F_\tau := [\theta_0 + l\tau,\ \pi - \theta_0 - l\tau], \qquad e_\tau(\theta_0) = \frac\omega\pi - s,
\end{equation}
and $e_\tau(\theta_0 + \tau x) = \omega/\pi + e(x)$ for $|\tau x| \le r_0$.

\emph{The density.} Let $f_0 := \pi^{-1}(1 - \tau\mathcal Ne_\tau)$ with $\mathcal N$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:shape}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:shape}(i), $\int_0^\pi f_0 = 1$ and $E_{f_0} = -\log 2 + \tau(e_\tau - \bar e_\tau)$ on $[0,\pi]$, with $\bar e_\tau := \pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi e_\tau$. Let $A$ be the set of $\vartheta \in [0,\pi]$ with $\operatorname{dist}(\vartheta,\{\theta_0,\pi-\theta_0\}) > r_0$. We claim that $f_0(\pi - \vartheta) = f_0(\vartheta)$ and that, with $C_1 := \pi^{-2}\bigl(1 + \cot(r_0/4) + \cot(\omega/4) + 2\cot(\theta_0/4)\bigr)$, for a.e.\ $\vartheta \in [0,\pi]$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:f0_inner}
\begin{aligned}
\Bigl|f_0(\vartheta) - m\Bigl(\frac{\vartheta - \theta_0}{\tau}\Bigr)\Bigr| &\le C_1\tau \quad \text{if } |\vartheta - \theta_0| \le r_0, \\
\Bigl|f_0(\vartheta) - \frac1\pi\Bigr| &\le C_1\tau \quad \text{if } \vartheta \in A .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The symmetry holds since the cosine coefficients of $e_\tau$ vanish for odd $k$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:shape}(ii) and the identity
\[
\frac{2\sin\varphi}{\cos\varphi - \cos\vartheta} = \cot\frac{\vartheta-\varphi}2 - \cot\frac{\vartheta+\varphi}2 ,
\]
for almost every $\vartheta$
\[
\tau\mathcal Ne_\tau(\vartheta) = \frac\tau{2\pi}\,\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int_0^\pi e_\tau'(\varphi)\Bigl(\cot\frac{\vartheta-\varphi}2 - \cot\frac{\vartheta+\varphi}2\Bigr)d\varphi ,
\]
where $e_\tau' = e_1 + e_2$ with $e_1(\varphi) := \tau^{-1}e'((\varphi - \theta_0)/\tau)$, supported in $V := [\theta_0 - g\tau, \theta_0 + l\tau]$, and $e_2(\varphi) := -e_1(\pi - \varphi)$, supported in $\pi - V$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:inner}(i), $\int|e_1| = \int|e_2| = 1$. For $\varphi \in V\cup(\pi - V)$ and $\vartheta \in [0,\pi]$ we have $\theta_0/2 \le \vartheta + \varphi \le 2\pi - \theta_0/2$, so $|\cot\frac{\vartheta+\varphi}2| \le \cot(\theta_0/4)$, and $|\cot\frac{\vartheta-\varphi}2| \le \cot(\rho/2)$ whenever $|\vartheta - \varphi| \ge \rho$, $0 < \rho \le \pi$. If $\vartheta \in A$, then $|\vartheta - \varphi| \ge r_0/2$ on $V \cup (\pi - V)$, since $(g + l)\tau \le r_0/2$, and $|\tau\mathcal Ne_\tau(\vartheta)| \le \pi^{-1}\tau(\cot(r_0/4) + \cot(\theta_0/4))$, which gives the second estimate. Let $|\vartheta - \theta_0| \le r_0$ and $u := (\vartheta - \theta_0)/\tau$. On $\pi - V$, $|\vartheta - \varphi| \ge \omega - r_0 - l\tau \ge \omega/2$, so the contribution of $e_2$ is at most $(2\pi)^{-1}\tau(\cot(\omega/4) + \cot(\theta_0/4))$, and that of $e_1$ with the second cotangent is at most $(2\pi)^{-1}\tau\cot(\theta_0/4)$. In the remaining term we write $\frac12\cot\frac x2 = \frac1x + k(x)$, where $k$ is odd and decreasing on $(-\pi,\pi)$, so that $|k| \le 1/\pi$ there, and substitute $\varphi = \theta_0 + \tau y$; as $|\vartheta - \varphi| \le r_0 + (g+l)\tau < \pi$ for $\varphi \in V$, Lemma~\ref{lem:inner}(ii) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac\tau{2\pi}\,\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int e_1(\varphi)\cot\frac{\vartheta-\varphi}2\,d\varphi &= \frac1\pi\,\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e'(y)}{u - y}\,dy + \frac\tau\pi\int e_1(\varphi)\,k(\vartheta-\varphi)\,d\varphi \\
&= 1 - \pi m(u) + R_1,
\end{aligned}
\]
with $|R_1| \le \tau/\pi^2$. Hence $|\tau\mathcal Ne_\tau(\vartheta) - 1 + \pi m(u)| \le \pi C_1\tau$, which is the first estimate.

\emph{The correction.} Let $Z_1 := [\theta_0 + x_\ast\tau,\ \theta_0 + l\tau]$, $Z := Z_1 \cup (\pi - Z_1)$ and $Y := [\theta_0, \theta_0 + l\tau] \cup [\pi - \theta_0 - l\tau, \pi - \theta_0] \subset Z$, so that $A \cap Z = \emptyset$ and $|A| = \pi - 4r_0 \ge \pi/2$. By \eqref{eq:f0_inner}, the symmetry of $f_0$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:inner}(iii), a.e.\ $f_0 \ge -C_1\tau$ on $Z$, $f_0 \ge 1/\omega - C_1\tau$ on $Y$, where $m = 1/\omega$, and $f_0 \ge 1/(2\pi) - C_1\tau$ on $[0,\pi]\setminus Z$, where $m \ge 1/(2\pi)$ in the first case of \eqref{eq:f0_inner}. Put
\[
f := f_0 + C_1\tau\,\mathbf 1_Z - \frac{C_1\tau|Z|}{|A|}\,\mathbf 1_A .
\]
Then $\int_0^\pi f = 1$, and for $\tau \le \tau_2 := \min\{\tau_1, 1/(4\pi C_1)\}$, since $|Z| \le |A|$, $f \ge 0$ a.e.\ on $[0,\pi]$ and $f \ge 1/\omega$ a.e.\ on $Y$. As $|Z| = 2(l - x_\ast)\tau$, $\tau \le 1$ and $|A| \ge \pi/2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:env}(b) gives $|E_f - E_{f_0}| \le C_1\tau C_0|Z|^{1/2} + C_1\tau|Z||A|^{-1/2}C_0 \le C_2\tau^{3/2}$ on $[0,\pi]$, with $C_2 := C_0C_1\bigl((2(l - x_\ast))^{1/2} + 2(2/\pi)^{1/2}(l - x_\ast)\bigr)$.

\emph{The admissible triple.} Let $\nu$ be the image of $f\,d\theta$ under $\theta \mapsto \cos\theta$, a positive measure on $[-1,1]$ of mass one, $F := \cos(F_\tau) \subset [-c_0,c_0]$ and $b_\tau := \log 2 + \tau\bar e_\tau - \tau\omega/\pi - C_2\tau^{3/2}$. Then
\[
b_\tau - U^\nu(\cos\vartheta) = b_\tau + E_f(\vartheta) = \tau\Bigl(e_\tau(\vartheta) - \frac\omega\pi\Bigr) + (E_f - E_{f_0})(\vartheta) - C_2\tau^{3/2},
\]
which by \eqref{eq:profile} is at most $0$ on $[0,\pi]$ and at most $-\tau$ on $F_\tau$; and $[-c_0,c_0]\setminus F$ is the image of $Y$ without its inner endpoints, where $f \ge 1/\omega$, so that $\nu \ge \mu_\omega$ there. Thus $(F, b_\tau, \nu)$ satisfies \eqref{eq:reduced_constraints}, and Proposition~\ref{prop:extremal} gives
\[
r_\omega(\tau) \ge b_\tau + E_f(\theta_0) \ge \tau\Bigl(e_\tau(\theta_0) - \frac\omega\pi\Bigr) - 2C_2\tau^{3/2} = -s\tau - 2C_2\tau^{3/2} \qquad (0 < \tau \le \tau_2).
\]

\emph{The upper bound.} Let $\omega' := \pi - \omega$ and $c := \omega/\omega'$. The lower bound for $\omega'$ gives $C'$ and $\tau' > 0$ with $r_{\omega'}(\sigma) \ge -s(\omega')\sigma - C'\sigma^{3/2}$ for $0 < \sigma \le \tau'$. Since $c\kappa_\sigma(\omega) = \kappa_\sigma(\omega')$, Theorem~\ref{thm:tail_duality}, applied at $\bar\tau = \tau/\kappa_\sigma(\omega)$, reads $r_\omega(\tau) = -\tau - c^{-1}r_{\omega'}(c\tau)$ for $0 < \tau < \kappa_\sigma(\omega)$, and $s(\omega') = \omega/\pi = 1 - s$; so for $0 < \tau \le \tau'/c$
\[
r_\omega(\tau) \le -\tau + s(\omega')\tau + C'c^{1/2}\tau^{3/2} = -s\tau + C'c^{1/2}\tau^{3/2}.
\]
Both bounds hold for $0 < \tau \le \tau_0 := \min\{\tau_2, \tau'/c\}$, which proves \eqref{eq:initial_slope} with the constant $\max\{2C_2, c^{1/2}C'\}$.

body_md: Let $v \in V_{N,d}$ vanish at the boundary nodes. On each face of $R_0$ the trace of $v$ lies in the tensor product of the one-dimensional spaces $V_N$ of the other $d-1$ directions and vanishes at the $N^{d-1}$ nodes of the face, at which interpolation in that space is unisolvent, its synthesis matrix being a Kronecker product of matrices that are nonsingular by Lemma~\ref{lem:lebesgue_condition_link}; hence $v = 0$ on $\partial R_0$, i.e.\ $v \in \Phi_{N,d}$. If moreover $\mathcal{L} v$ vanishes at the interior nodes, then $\mathcal{L} v = 0$ by the unisolvence, $v = 0$ on $\bar R_0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:dirichlet_box}(ii), and the coefficients of $v$ vanish because $\mathbf{W}_d$ is nonsingular; so $\mathbf{A}$ is nonsingular, and $u_N$ exists and lies in $\Phi_{N,d}$. The interior collocation equations then give $\mathcal{L} u_N = \mathcal{P}_{N,d}f$, exactly as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:representation}, and uniqueness is Lemma~\ref{lem:dirichlet_box}(ii). The function $u - u_N \in C^2(R_0)\cap C(\bar R_0)$ vanishes on $\partial R_0$ and satisfies $\mathcal{L}(u - u_N) = f - \mathcal{P}_{N,d}f$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:dirichlet_box}(ii) gives $\lVertu - u_N\rVert_\infty \le (e^{\alpha L_1}-1)\lVertf - \mathcal{P}_{N,d}f\rVert_\infty$, and $\lVertf - \mathcal{P}_{N,d}f\rVert_\infty \le (1 + \Lambda(\Psi_{N,d}))\operatorname{dist}_\infty(f,\Psi_{N,d})$ as in Corollary~\ref{cor:error}. For the second bound, $\sum_m|(\mathbf{G}_N)_{im}| = \sum_m s_m(\mathbf{G}_N)_{im}$ with $s_m := \operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{G}_N)_{im}$ is the value at $\mathbf x_i$ of the collocation solution for the interior data $(s_m)_m$, whose interpolant $\sum_m s_m\ell_m^\Psi$ in $\Psi_{N,d}$ has supremum norm at most $\Lambda(\Psi_{N,d})$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:dirichlet_box}(ii) to that solution. For the last claim, the same face argument shows that $v \in V_{N,d}$ lies in $\Phi_{N,d}$ if and only if it vanishes at the $N^d - (N-2)^d$ boundary nodes, whose evaluation functionals are linearly independent on $V_{N,d}$ because $\mathbf{W}_d$ is nonsingular; so $\dim\Phi_{N,d} = (N-2)^d$, and the $(N-2)^d$ linearly independent products of the one-dimensional bases, which vanish on $\partial R_0$, form a basis of $\Phi_{N,d}$. Moreover $\mathcal{L}^{-1}$ enters the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:regularized} only through the identity $u - u_N^\varepsilon = \mathcal{L}^{-1}(f - \mathcal{L} u_N^\varepsilon)$, which here expresses uniqueness, and through its $L^2$ norm, which Lemma~\ref{lem:dirichlet_box}(iii) bounds; the remaining steps are unchanged.

label: rem:relocation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:relocation}
For a domain $\Omega \subset R_0$ with smooth boundary $\Gamma$, the extended-domain solver of \cite{wu2018development} keeps the tensor-product basis and the tensor-product grid, moves the grid nodes adjacent to $\Gamma$ onto $\Gamma$, imposes the boundary data at the moved nodes, and enforces the differential equation at all remaining nodes of $R_0$, inside and outside $\Omega$. For every grid edge that $\Gamma$ crosses, the endpoint nearer to $\Gamma$ is moved, in \cite{wu2018development} to a nearby point of a fine parametrization of $\Gamma$ and in the computations of Section~\ref{sec:num_disk} to the crossing point itself, in both cases by at most half a grid spacing. This requires the forcing to be defined on all of $R_0$; for manufactured solutions it is, and for general data a smooth extension of $f$ to $R_0$ must be constructed first, for instance a periodic $C^\infty$ extension to a rectangle \cite{boyd2005fourier, bueno2006fourier} or a $C^k$ extension obtained by solving a polyharmonic problem outside $\Omega$ \cite[Sec.~2.1]{stein2016immersed}. The continuous problem behind this formulation is uniquely solvable in $\Omega$ but not outside, and Theorem~\ref{thm:representation_d} does not cover it: the boundary data are imposed only at the relocated nodes, not on all of $\Gamma$, and the problem outside $\Omega$ carries no boundary condition. Node relocation changes the sampling set of the frame, not the frame; Section~\ref{sec:num_disk} tests its effect.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:pitfall}
The convergence rate and the accuracy floor of a Fourier extension depend on the extension ratio $\delta/L$ and on the extendability of the solution, so a comparison of operators on different domains or with different exact solutions cannot isolate the operator. A more insidious error is a solution that lies in the trial space: on $(0,1)$ the function $\sin(2\pi x)$ is a multiple of $w_{2(1+2\delta)}$ whenever $2\delta \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\sin(\pi x)$ one of $w_{1+2\delta}$ whenever $\delta\in\mathbb{N}$, so both are reproduced to machine precision by any operator as soon as $N$ reaches the mode index, regardless of conditioning. All solutions used below lie in no $V_N$.

label: lem:dirichlet_1d
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: The One-Dimensional Dirichlet Problem

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Let $\alpha := \lVertk\rVert_{L^\infty(I)} + 1$ and $v_\varepsilon := v + \varepsilon e^{\alpha x}$ for $\varepsilon > 0$. Then $\mathcal{L} v_\varepsilon = \mathcal{L} v + \varepsilon\alpha\bigl(k(x) - \alpha\bigr)e^{\alpha x} \le -\varepsilon\alpha e^{\alpha x} < 0$ on $I$. If $v_\varepsilon$ attained its maximum over $\bar I$ at a point $x_0 \in I$, then $v_\varepsilon'(x_0) = 0$ and $v_\varepsilon''(x_0) \le 0$, so $\mathcal{L} v_\varepsilon(x_0) = -v_\varepsilon''(x_0) \ge 0$, a contradiction. Hence $\max_{\bar I}v \le \max_{\bar I}v_\varepsilon = \max\{v_\varepsilon(0), v_\varepsilon(L)\} \le \max\{v(0),v(L)\} + \varepsilon e^{\alpha L}$, and $\varepsilon \to 0$ gives the first claim. If $\mathcal{L} v = 0$, the first claim applies to $v$ and to $-v$; if moreover $v(0) = v(L) = 0$, both bounds give $v \equiv 0$.

(ii) Uniqueness: the difference of two solutions satisfies (i) with zero boundary values. Existence: $E$ is strictly increasing with $E(0) = 0$, and $\mathcal{L} v = g$ is equivalent to $(e^{-K}v')' = -e^{-K}g$ because $K' = k$. Splitting the integral at $y = x$,
\[
v(x) = \frac{E(L) - E(x)}{E(L)}\int_0^x e^{-K(y)}E(y)\,g(y)\,dy + \frac{E(x)}{E(L)}\int_x^L e^{-K(y)}\bigl(E(L)-E(y)\bigr)g(y)\,dy .
\]
Differentiating, the two terms produced by the variable limits cancel, and with $E' = e^{K}$ one obtains $e^{-K(x)}v'(x) = E(L)^{-1}\bigl[-\int_0^x e^{-K}Eg + \int_x^L e^{-K}(E(L)-E)g\bigr] = c - \int_0^x e^{-K}g$, where $c := E(L)^{-1}\int_0^L e^{-K}(E(L) - E)g$. Differentiating once more gives $(e^{-K}v')' = -e^{-K}g$, so $\mathcal{L} v = g$; $v(0) = v(L) = 0$ because $E(0) = 0$ and $E(L) - E(L) = 0$; and $v' = e^{K}(c - \int_0^x e^{-K}g) \in C^1(\bar I)$, so $v \in C^2(\bar I)$.

(iii) $G \ge 0$ and continuous because $E$ is continuous and increasing with $E(0) = 0$. For $g \in C(\bar I)$, $|\mathcal{L}^{-1}g(x)| \le \lVertg\rVert_\infty\int_0^L G(x,y)\,dy$ with equality for $g \equiv 1$, and $\int_0^L G(x,y)\,dy = (\mathcal{L}^{-1}\mathbf 1)(x)$ by (ii). The $L^2$ bound is the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality applied to the integral kernel.

label: lem:cl2
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Elementary Properties of the Clausen Function

title: Proof
body_md:
Items (i) and (ii) and the first expansion in (iii) are Eqs.~(4.10)--(4.12), (4.17), (4.18) and (4.28) of \cite{lewin1981polylogarithms}; we include short proofs. Oddness holds because the integrand $h(t) := \log|2\sin(t/2)|$ is even. The identity $\int_0^\pi\log\sin u\,du = -\pi\log 2$ follows from $I := \int_0^\pi\log\sin u\,du = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\log\sin u\,du = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\log\cos u\,du$, whence $2I = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\log(\sin u\cos u)\,du = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\log\bigl(\tfrac12\sin 2u\bigr)\,du = -\pi\log 2 + I$. Hence $\int_0^\pi h = \pi\log 2 + 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\log\sin u\,du = 0$, i.e.\ $\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi) = 0$; since $h$ is $2\pi$-periodic and even, $\int_\pi^{2\pi}h = \int_0^\pi h = 0$, so $h$ has zero mean over a period, $\mathrm{Cl}_2$ is $2\pi$-periodic, and $\mathrm{Cl}_2(2\pi - x) = \mathrm{Cl}_2(-x) = -\mathrm{Cl}_2(x)$, which proves (i).

(ii) Substituting $t = 2s$ and using $2\sin s = (2\sin(s/2))(2\cos(s/2))$,
\begin{gather*}
\mathrm{Cl}_2(2x) = -2\int_0^x\log|2\sin s|\,ds = 2\mathrm{Cl}_2(x) - 2\int_0^x\log|2\cos(s/2)|\,ds, \\
\int_0^x\log|2\cos(s/2)|\,ds = \int_{\pi-x}^{\pi}\log|2\sin(u/2)|\,du = \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi-x) - \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi) ,
\end{gather*}
by $s = \pi - u$; with (i) this is the duplication formula, and $x = \pi/3$ gives $\mathrm{Cl}_2(2\pi/3) = 2\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi/3) - 2\mathrm{Cl}_2(2\pi/3)$.

(iii) For $0 < t \le 1$, $\log(2\sin(t/2)) = \log t + \log\bigl(\sin(t/2)/(t/2)\bigr) = \log t + O(t^2)$, so $\mathrm{Cl}_2(x) = -\int_0^x\log t\,dt + O(x^3) = x - x\log x + O(x^3)$. Also $\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi - x) = \mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi) + \int_{\pi-x}^{\pi}h = \int_0^x\log(2\cos(s/2))\,ds = \int_0^x\bigl(\log 2 + O(s^2)\bigr)ds = x\log 2 + O(x^3)$.

(iv) Since $|\cos\theta - \cos\varphi| = \tfrac12\,|2\sin\tfrac{\varphi+\theta}{2}|\,|2\sin\tfrac{\varphi-\theta}{2}|$,
\[
\int_0^\pi\log|\cos\theta - \cos\varphi|\,d\varphi = -\pi\log 2 + \int_\theta^{\pi+\theta}h(t)\,dt + \int_{-\theta}^{\pi-\theta}h(t)\,dt ,
\]
by the substitutions $t = \varphi + \theta$ and $t = \varphi - \theta$. The substitution $t \mapsto 2\pi - t$ and the evenness and periodicity of $h$ turn the first integral into $\int_{\pi-\theta}^{2\pi-\theta}h$, so the two integrals add up to $\int_{-\theta}^{2\pi-\theta}h$, the integral over a full period, which vanishes by (i).

label: lem:riemann
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Riemann Sums with a Logarithmic Singularity

label: eq:riemann_split
title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Decomposition.} Since $\cos\vartheta - \cos\varphi = 2\sin\tfrac12(\varphi+\vartheta)\sin\tfrac12(\varphi-\vartheta)$,
\[
g_\vartheta = \log 2 + h_1 + h_2, \qquad h_1(\varphi) := \log\bigl|\sin\tfrac12(\varphi - \vartheta)\bigr|, \quad h_2(\varphi) := \log\bigl|\sin\tfrac12(\varphi+\vartheta)\bigr| .
\]
Let $I_m := [\theta_m - \Delta/2, \theta_m + \Delta/2]$ and $J := \bigcup_{m=1}^N I_m = [\theta_0 - \Delta/2, \pi - \theta_0 + \Delta/2]$; the cells are adjacent and $\int_{I_m}\log 2 = \Delta\log 2$ for every $m$, so the constant term cancels cell by cell and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:riemann_split}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\sum_{m=1}^N g_\vartheta(\theta_m) - \int_{\theta_0}^{\pi-\theta_0}g_\vartheta
&= \sum_{m=1}^N\Bigl(\Delta h_1(\theta_m) - \int_{I_m}h_1\Bigr) + \sum_{m=1}^N\Bigl(\Delta h_2(\theta_m) - \int_{I_m}h_2\Bigr) \\
&\quad + \Bigl(\int_J g_\vartheta - \int_{\theta_0}^{\pi-\theta_0}g_\vartheta\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In case (b) the term $m = j$ is removed from the left-hand sum; this removes $\Delta h_1(\theta_j)$ and $\Delta h_2(\theta_j)$ from the two sums and adds $-\Delta\log 2$ to the right-hand side. Note that in case (b) the index $j$ is unique, since the nodes are $\Delta$ apart. We use the midpoint rule $|\Delta\,h(\theta_m) - \int_{I_m}h| \le (\Delta^3/24)\max_{I_m}|h''|$ for $h \in C^2(I_m)$, and we bound the three brackets of \eqref{eq:riemann_split} in turn; $C$ denotes constants depending only on $\theta_0$.

\emph{The smooth term $h_2$.} Since $\Delta \le \theta_0$, $J \subset [\theta_0/2, \pi - \theta_0/2]$, and the second elementary fact gives $\sin\tfrac12(\varphi+\vartheta) \ge \sin(\theta_0/4)$ for $\varphi \in J$, $\vartheta \in [0,\pi]$. Hence $h_2 \in C^2(J)$ with $|h_2| \le \log(1/\sin(\theta_0/4))$ and $|h_2''(\varphi)| = \bigl(4\sin^2\tfrac12(\varphi+\vartheta)\bigr)^{-1} \le \bigl(4\sin^2(\theta_0/4)\bigr)^{-1}$, so the second bracket is at most $N\Delta^3C \le C\Delta^2$, because $N\Delta = \omega + \Delta \le 2\omega$. In case (b) the missing term contributes in addition $|\int_{I_j}h_2| \le C\Delta$.

\emph{The singular term $h_1$: cells away from $\vartheta$.} For $\varphi \in J \subset (0,\pi)$ and $\vartheta \in [0,\pi]$ one has $|\varphi - \vartheta| < \pi$, so $h_1$ is smooth on $J$ except at $\varphi = \vartheta$, and for $\varphi \ne \vartheta$ the first elementary fact gives $|h_1''(\varphi)| = \bigl(4\sin^2\tfrac12(\varphi-\vartheta)\bigr)^{-1} \le \pi^2/(4|\varphi-\vartheta|^2)$. Let $\mathcal M := \{m : |\theta_m - \vartheta| \le 3\Delta/2\}$, a set of at most four indices, since an interval of length $3\Delta$ contains at most four points spaced $\Delta$ apart. For $m \notin \mathcal M$ and $\varphi \in I_m$, $|\varphi - \vartheta| \ge |\theta_m - \vartheta| - \Delta/2 \ge \tfrac23|\theta_m - \vartheta| > 0$, so $h_1 \in C^2(I_m)$ and the midpoint error on $I_m$ is at most $(\Delta^3/24)\cdot\tfrac{9\pi^2}{16}|\theta_m - \vartheta|^{-2}$. On either side of $\vartheta$, the nodes outside $\mathcal M$ are at distances greater than $3\Delta/2$ that increase in steps of $\Delta$, so the $k$-th of them is at distance at least $k\Delta/2$; hence $\sum_{m\notin\mathcal M}|\theta_m - \vartheta|^{-2} \le 2\sum_{k\ge1}(k\Delta/2)^{-2} = (4\pi^2/3)\Delta^{-2} \le 14\Delta^{-2}$, and the cells outside $\mathcal M$ contribute at most $C\Delta$ to the first bracket.

\emph{The singular term $h_1$: cells near $\vartheta$.} For $m \in \mathcal M$ we bound $\Delta|h_1(\theta_m)|$ and $\int_{I_m}|h_1|$ separately. In case (a), $\Delta/4 \le |\theta_m - \vartheta| \le 3\Delta/2 \le \pi$, so the first elementary fact gives $|\sin\tfrac12(\theta_m-\vartheta)| \ge \Delta/(4\pi)$ and therefore $0 \le -h_1(\theta_m) \le \log(4\pi/\Delta)$; in case (b) the same holds for $m \in \mathcal M\setminus\{j\}$, because then $|\theta_m - \vartheta| \ge |\theta_m - \theta_j| - |\theta_j - \vartheta| \ge 3\Delta/4$, and the term $m = j$ does not occur. For $\varphi \in I_m$, $m \in \mathcal M$, one has $|\varphi - \vartheta| \le 2\Delta \le \pi$, hence $0 \le -h_1(\varphi) \le \log\bigl(\pi/|\varphi-\vartheta|\bigr)$ and
\[
\int_{I_m}|h_1| \le \int_{|s|\le 2\Delta}\log\frac{\pi}{|s|}\,ds = 4\Delta\Bigl(1 + \log\frac{\pi}{2\Delta}\Bigr).
\]
Hence the cells in $\mathcal M$ contribute at most $4\bigl[\Delta\log(4\pi/\Delta) + 4\Delta(1 + \log(\pi/(2\Delta)))\bigr] \le C\Delta\log(1/\Delta)$ to the first bracket, in both cases.

\emph{The ends and the omitted cell.} The third bracket of \eqref{eq:riemann_split} is the integral of $g_\vartheta$ over the two half-cells $[\theta_0 - \Delta/2, \theta_0]$ and $[\pi-\theta_0, \pi-\theta_0+\Delta/2]$, which lie in $J$; on each, $|g_\vartheta| \le \log 2 + |h_1| + C$, and the integral of $|h_1|$ over an interval of length $\Delta/2$ contained in $J$ is at most $\int_{|s|\le\Delta}\log(\pi/|s|)\,ds = 2\Delta(1 + \log(\pi/\Delta))$, because $-h_1(\varphi) \le \log(\pi/|\varphi - \vartheta|)$ on $J$ and the right-hand side is a decreasing function of $|\varphi-\vartheta|$. So the third bracket is at most $C\Delta\log(1/\Delta)$. In case (b) the additional term $\Delta\log 2$ is of the same order. Collecting the bounds proves the lemma.

title: Proof
body_md: By the symmetry $U_\omega(\cos(\pi-\theta)) = U_\omega(\cos\theta)$, and by splitting at $\pi/2$ an interval that contains $\pi/2$, it suffices to take $\vartheta, \vartheta' \in [0,\pi/2]$. For $\theta \in (0,\pi/2)\setminus\{\theta_0\}$ the derivative formula in Step~4 of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:clausen} gives $|\tfrac{d}{d\theta}U_\omega(\cos\theta)| \le \omega^{-1}\bigl(|\log\sin(\theta+\theta_0)| + |\log\sin|\theta-\theta_0||\bigr)$. Here $\theta+\theta_0 \in [\theta_0, \pi/2+\theta_0]$, so $\sin(\theta+\theta_0) \ge \min\{\sin\theta_0, \cos\theta_0\}$ and the first term is bounded by a constant; and $|\theta-\theta_0| \le \pi/2$, so $\sin|\theta-\theta_0| \ge 2|\theta-\theta_0|/\pi$ and the second term is at most $\log\bigl(\pi/(2|\theta-\theta_0|)\bigr)$. Since $\theta \mapsto U_\omega(\cos\theta)$ is continuous on $[0,\pi/2]$ and continuously differentiable off $\theta_0$ with integrable derivative, it is absolutely continuous, and $|U_\omega(\cos\vartheta) - U_\omega(\cos\vartheta')|$ is at most the integral of this bound over the interval between $\vartheta$ and $\vartheta'$, of length $s := |\vartheta - \vartheta'| \le 1/2$. The integral of $\log(\pi/(2|\theta - \theta_0|))$ over an interval of length $s$ is largest when the interval is centred at $\theta_0$, where it equals $2\int_0^{s/2}\log\bigl(\pi/(2u)\bigr)\,du = s\bigl(1 + \log(\pi/s)\bigr)$. This gives \eqref{eq:U_modulus}.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:chebyshev_variable}, $\ell_m^V(x) = (\sin\theta/\sin\theta_m)\,\ell_m(\cos\theta)$: this function lies in $V_N = \sqrt{2/\tilde L}\sin\theta\cdot\mathbb P_{N-1}(z)$ and equals $\delta_{mk}$ at $\theta_k$. Since $dx = (\tilde L/\pi)\,d\theta$ and $\sin\theta_0 \le \sin\theta_m \le 1$,
\begin{gather*}
\lVert\ell_m^V\rVert_{L^2(\tilde I)}^2 = \frac{\tilde L}{\pi\sin^2\theta_m}\int_0^\pi \sin^2\theta\,\ell_m(\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta, \\
\lVert\ell_m^V\rVert_{L^2(I)}^2 = \frac{\tilde L}{\pi\sin^2\theta_m}\int_{\theta_0}^{\pi-\theta_0}\sin^2\theta\,\ell_m(\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta .
\end{gather*}
\emph{Upper bounds.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:lagrange_polynomials}(a) and Lemma~\ref{lem:clausen}, $\max_{[-1,1]}|\ell_m|^2 \le \exp\bigl(2N[U_\omega(z_m) - U_\omega(1)] + C\log N\bigr)$ and $\max_{[-c_0,c_0]}|\ell_m|^2 \le \exp\bigl(2N[U_\omega(z_m) - U_\omega(c_0)] + C\log N\bigr)$, because $U_\omega$ attains its minimum over $[-1,1]$ at $\pm1$ and over $[-c_0,c_0]$ at $\pm c_0$. Both integrals are bounded by $\pi$ times these maxima, so that the squared norms are at most $\tilde L/\sin^2\theta_0$ times them, and $\lVert\ell_m^V\rVert_{L^\infty(I)} \le \max_{[-c_0,c_0]}|\ell_m|/\sin\theta_0$.

\emph{Lower bounds.} For the extended interval, restrict the integral to $\theta \in [1/N, 2/N]$, which for $N \ge N_0$ lies outside $[\theta_0 - \Delta/4, \pi]$, so that Lemma~\ref{lem:lagrange_polynomials}(b) applies; there $\sin^2\theta \ge (2/(\pi N))^2$ and, by \eqref{eq:U_modulus}, $U_\omega(\cos\theta) \le U_\omega(1) + C\log N/N$. Hence, as $\tilde L/(\pi\sin^2\theta_m) \ge \tilde L/\pi$, $\lVert\ell_m^V\rVert^2_{L^2(\tilde I)} \ge (\tilde L/\pi)N^{-1}(2/(\pi N))^2\exp\bigl(2N[U_\omega(z_m) - U_\omega(1)] - C\log N\bigr)$. For the physical interval, restrict to $\theta \in [\theta_0 + \Delta/4, \theta_0 + 3\Delta/4]$, an interval of length $\Delta/2$ inside $[\theta_0,\pi-\theta_0]$ at distance at least $\Delta/4$ from every node; there $\sin^2\theta \ge \sin^2\theta_0$ and $U_\omega(\cos\theta) \le U_\omega(c_0) + C\Delta\log(1/\Delta)$ by \eqref{eq:U_modulus}, so $\lVert\ell_m^V\rVert^2_{L^2(I)} \ge (\tilde L/\pi)(\Delta/2)\sin^2\theta_0\exp\bigl(2N[U_\omega(z_m) - U_\omega(c_0)] - C\log N\bigr)$, and the same evaluation point gives the lower bound for the supremum norm. Taking logarithms and dividing by $N$ proves \eqref{eq:lagrange_norms}, the factors $\tilde L$, $\sin\theta_0$ and $\Delta$ contributing $O(\log N/N)$ with constants depending only on $\delta$ and $L$.

title: Lemma

name: Nodal Norms of Shifted Sines

title: Proof
body_md:
We distinguish three ranges of $J$.

\emph{(i) $J\Delta \ge \pi/4$.} Since $J\Delta \le N\Delta = \omega + \Delta \le \pi - 7\theta_0/4$ for $\Delta \le \theta_0/4$, the number $J\Delta$ lies in $[\pi/4, \pi - 7\theta_0/4]$ (if this interval is empty, which happens for $\theta_0 > 3\pi/7$, there is no such $J$ and nothing to prove), and on it $\sin(J\Delta) \ge s^\ast := \min\{\sin(\pi/4), \sin(7\theta_0/4)\} > 0$, since $\sin$ is concave on $[0,\pi]$. Writing $\sin^2 x = \tfrac12 - \tfrac12\cos 2x$ and $\theta_m = \theta_2 + (m-2)\Delta$,
\[
\sum_{m=2}^{N-1}\sin^2(J\theta_m + \beta) = \frac{N-2}{2} - \frac12\,\mathrm{Re}\Bigl[e^{2i(J\theta_2+\beta)}\,\frac{e^{2iJ\Delta(N-2)} - 1}{e^{2iJ\Delta} - 1}\Bigr],
\]
where $e^{2iJ\Delta} \ne 1$ because $2J\Delta \in (0,2\pi)$; the bracket has modulus at most $2/|e^{2iJ\Delta} - 1| = 1/\sin(J\Delta) \le 1/s^\ast$. Hence the sum is at least $(N-2)/2 - 1/(2s^\ast) \ge (N-2)/4 \ge N/8$ for $N \ge \max\{4, 2 + 2/s^\ast\}$.

\emph{(ii) $J \ge 4\pi/\omega$ and $J\Delta < \pi/4$.} The set $\{\theta \in \mathbb R : \sin^2(J\theta + \beta) \ge 1/2\}$ is the union of the intervals $H_i := \bigl[(i\pi + \pi/4 - \beta)/J,\ (i\pi + 3\pi/4 - \beta)/J\bigr]$, $i \in \mathbb Z$, each of length $\pi/(2J)$, whose left endpoints form a lattice of spacing $\pi/J$. The interval $H_i$ lies inside the arc $[\theta_0,\pi-\theta_0]$ whenever its left endpoint lies in $[\theta_0, \pi - \theta_0 - \pi/(2J)]$, an interval of length $\omega - \pi/(2J) \ge 0$, which contains at least $\lfloor(\omega - \pi/(2J))J/\pi\rfloor \ge \omega J/\pi - 2 \ge \omega J/(2\pi)$ lattice points because $\omega J/\pi \ge 4$. Each such $H_i$ has length $\pi/(2J) \ge 2\Delta$ and therefore contains at least $\lfloor\pi/(2J\Delta)\rfloor \ge \pi/(4J\Delta)$ of the nodes $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_N$, which are the points of the lattice $\theta_0 + \Delta\mathbb Z$ in the arc (an interval of length $\ell \ge 2\Delta$ contains at least $\lfloor\ell/\Delta\rfloor \ge \ell/(2\Delta)$ points of a lattice of spacing $\Delta$). Hence at least $(\omega J/2\pi)\cdot\pi/(4J\Delta) = \omega/(8\Delta) = (N-1)/8$ nodes satisfy $\sin^2(J\theta_m+\beta) \ge 1/2$, all but at most two of them interior, and the sum is at least $\tfrac12\bigl((N-1)/8 - 2\bigr) \ge N/64$ for $N \ge 65$.

\emph{(iii) $3 \le J < 4\pi/\omega$.} There are finitely many such $J$, independently of $N$. For each of them and each $\beta$, the function $\phi_{J,\beta}(\theta) := \sin^2(J\theta + \beta)$ is continuous and nonnegative and vanishes only at isolated points, so $\mathcal I_J(\beta) := \int_{\theta_0}^{\pi-\theta_0}\phi_{J,\beta}\,d\theta > 0$; since $\mathcal I_J$ is continuous and $2\pi$-periodic in $\beta$, $I_J := \min_\beta \mathcal I_J(\beta) > 0$. The sum $\Delta\sum_{m=2}^{N-1}\phi_{J,\beta}(\theta_m)$ is the rectangle rule with cells of length $\Delta$ centred at the interior nodes, which cover $[\theta_0 + \Delta/2, \pi - \theta_0 - \Delta/2]$; its error against $\int_{\theta_0}^{\pi-\theta_0}\phi_{J,\beta}$ is at most $\Delta$ times the total variation of $\phi_{J,\beta}$ on the arc, plus the integral over the two uncovered half-cells, hence at most $\Delta(2J\omega/\pi + 3)$, because the extrema of $\phi_{J,\beta}$ are the points with $J\theta + \beta \in \tfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbb Z$, spaced $\pi/(2J)$ apart, so that $\phi_{J,\beta}$ has at most $2J\omega/\pi + 2$ monotone pieces on the arc, each of variation at most one, and $\phi_{J,\beta} \le 1$. Consequently $\sum_{m=2}^{N-1}\phi_{J,\beta}(\theta_m) \ge \bigl(I_J - \Delta(2J\omega/\pi + 3)\bigr)/\Delta \ge I_J/(2\Delta) = I_J(N-1)/(2\omega) \ge I_J N/(4\omega)$ as soon as $\Delta \le I_J/(2(2J\omega/\pi + 3))$ and $N \ge 2$.

The lemma holds with $c_S := \min\{1/64,\ \min_{3 \le J < 4\pi/\omega} I_J/(4\omega)\}$ and $N_0$ the largest of the thresholds in (i)--(iii).

title: Proof
body_md:
The coefficients of Section~\ref{sec:constants} are $a_j = s_J/s_1$, $b_j = 0$ for odd $J$ and $a_j = 0$, $b_j = s_J/s_2$ for even $J$, with $s_i = \sin(i\theta_0)$; in particular $|a_j| \le 1/\sin\theta_0$, $|b_j| \le 1/\sin 2\theta_0$, and we put $A := \max\{1/\sin\theta_0, 1/\sin 2\theta_0\}$. By \eqref{eq:Lw_nodes},
\begin{gather*}
(\mathbf{B})_{mj} = \psi_j(x_m) = \sqrt{2/\tilde L}\;\rho_J\bigl[\sin(J\theta_m + \vartheta_J) - g_J(\theta_m)\bigr], \\
g_J(\theta) := \frac{a_j\rho_1\sin(\theta + \vartheta_1) + b_j\rho_2\sin(2\theta + \vartheta_2)}{\rho_J},
\end{gather*}
and $|g_J| \le A(\rho_1 + \rho_2)/\rho_J \le A(\rho_1+\rho_2)\tilde L^2/(\pi^2J^2) =: A_k/J^2$, because $\rho_J \ge \lambda_J$. The upper bound in \eqref{eq:column_norms} follows with $C_B := \sqrt{2/\tilde L}\,(1 + A_k/9)$. For the lower bound, the triangle inequality in $\ell^2$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:nodal_sines} give
\[
\lVert\mathbf{B}\mathbf{e}_j\rVert_2 \ge \sqrt{2/\tilde L}\;\rho_J\Bigl(\sqrt{c_SN} - \sqrt{N}\,\frac{A_k}{J^2}\Bigr) \ge \sqrt{2/\tilde L}\;\rho_J\,\frac{\sqrt{c_SN}}{2}
\]
for $J \ge J_1 := \bigl\lceil (2A_k/\sqrt{c_S})^{1/2}\bigr\rceil$.
For the finitely many $J$ with $3 \le J < J_1$ the function $\theta \mapsto \sin(J\theta + \vartheta_J) - g_J(\theta)$ does not depend on $N$ and is a nonzero trigonometric polynomial, its component of frequency $J$ having coefficient one, so $I'_J := \int_{\theta_0}^{\pi-\theta_0}\bigl(\sin(J\theta+\vartheta_J) - g_J(\theta)\bigr)^2d\theta > 0$, and the rectangle-rule estimate of case (iii) of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:nodal_sines}, applied to the square of this function, which is continuous, of bounded variation and bounded by $(1 + A_k/9)^2$ on the arc, with its own variation and maximum in place of those of $\phi_{J,\beta}$, gives $\sum_{m=2}^{N-1}\bigl(\sin(J\theta_m + \vartheta_J) - g_J(\theta_m)\bigr)^2 \ge I'_JN/(4\omega)$ for $N \ge N_J$, where $N_J$ depends only on $J$, $\theta_0$, $L$ and $k$. The lower bound in \eqref{eq:column_norms} holds with $c_B := \sqrt{2/\tilde L}\,\min\bigl\{\sqrt{c_S}/2,\ \min_{3\le J<J_1}(I'_J/(4\omega))^{1/2}\bigr\}$ and $N_0$ the maximum of the threshold of Lemma~\ref{lem:nodal_sines} and of the finitely many $N_J$.
